LAYER ONE Field guide Edition 1.0 — Complete

The first layer is the one everything else stands on.

The Design Systems Playbook

A complete, plain-language guide to design systems: why they matter, how to build their foundations, components and patterns, and how to run them for years. For anyone starting from zero.

AuthorAniket Pandey
Published byLayer One, Bangalore
Weblayerone.co.in
Year2026

Before you start

A guide for anyone who needs to understand design systems, starting from zero.

Most writing about design systems is either a sales pitch or a technical tutorial. Neither helps a founder decide whether to invest, a product manager understand what their design team is asking for, or a new designer see how all the pieces fit together. This book tries to do exactly that.

We've written it the way we'd explain things across a table: in plain language, with real situations, and with the reasoning behind every recommendation. If you've never worked with a design system, you should be able to follow every page. If you've worked with them for years, we hope you'll still find useful frameworks, honest numbers and a few new angles, especially on the day-to-day work of running a system.

It's written by Aniket Pandey, who leads Layer One, a design systems studio in Bangalore. Aniket has built design systems at IBM (for clients including Cardinal Health and Riyadh Air), led the design system at CARS24 across 10+ products in three countries, and works on design system tooling and governance at JPMorgan Chase.1 The book combines that experience with the published work of practitioners such as Nathan Curtis, Brad Frost, Ben Callahan, Dan Mall and Alla Kholmatova, and with the public documentation of mature systems from IBM, Google, Atlassian, Adobe, Salesforce and the UK government.

How sure are we? Four labels

Not everything in this book is equally certain, and we think you deserve to know which is which. Claims that matter carry one of four labels:

Standard
A formal standard, like the accessibility guidelines (WCAG 2.2). If you need to comply, it's not optional.
Documented
Published research, a case study or official documentation. Always cited, with a warning when the study is small or run by a vendor.
Practice
Our recommendation from practice. Reasoned and tested, but not universal. Disagree if your situation is different.
Illustrative
A worked example built on stated assumptions. It shows a method, not a measured result.

We don't invent statistics, case studies or results. Worked examples use Ledgerly, a fictional business finance product, so you never confuse an illustration with a real client. Every colour value, contrast ratio and type size in the figures is calculated by the book's build script, not typed by hand.

Chapter 01

01

What a design system actually is

Most people picture a design system as a Figma file full of buttons. That's part of it, but only a small part. Let's start from the beginning, with a situation you've probably already lived through.

Read this if

You keep hearing "design system" and you're not sure everyone means the same thing, including you.

What you'll leave with
  1. A plain-English definition you can repeat to anyone.
  2. The difference between a style guide, a UI kit, a component library and a design system.
  3. Why a design system matters more and more as a company grows.

In this chapter

  1. 01.1The five-button problem
  2. 01.2A definition you can actually use
  3. 01.3Style guide, UI kit, component library, design system

01.1The five-button problem

Picture a product team with five designers. Each of them is working on a different part of the app: one on onboarding, one on billing, one on settings, and so on. None of them is careless. Each one designs a good-looking button for their screens.

A year later, someone counts. The app has five slightly different primary buttons. They're all roughly blue. One has rounded corners, one is a bit taller, one uses a bolder font, one turns a darker blue on hover and another turns lighter. Engineering has built each of them separately, because each designer handed over a different spec.

Nobody decided to have five buttons. It just happened, one reasonable decision at a time.

Now the company changes its brand colour. Somebody has to find all five buttons, in every screen, in design files and in code, and update each one. They'll miss a few. The product will look a little off for months. And the same thing has quietly happened to text styles, form fields, spacing, error messages and icons.

Scenario"Why does our app look like three different companies built it?"
The situation

A growing SaaS company has three product squads. Each squad has its own designer and its own engineers, and each one moves fast.

What goes wrong

Every squad solves the same problems slightly differently: tables, filters, empty screens, error messages. Customers notice. So does the sales team during demos.

What a design system changes

The squads agree on one way to do the common things, build those once, and share them. Each squad spends its time on what makes its part of the product unique.

That, in one story, is why design systems exist. They're not about making things pretty. They're about making sure that many people, working in parallel, end up building one product instead of several that happen to share a logo.

01.2A definition you can actually use

Here's the definition we use with clients. It's deliberately simple:

In one sentence

A design system is a shared set of decisions, reusable parts and working agreements that helps many people build one consistent product, plus the people and process that keep it up to date.

Let's unpack the three ingredients, because most design systems that fail are missing one of them.

01 · Decisions

"What we've agreed"

Which colours we use and for what. How big our text is. How much space goes between things. How we write error messages. The reasons behind the look.

02 · Reusable parts

"What we've built"

Ready-made buttons, inputs, menus and tables, available to designers in their design tool and to engineers in code, plus guidance on how to use them.

03 · Agreements

"How we work together"

Who looks after the system, how people ask for new things, how changes are announced, and what happens when two teams want different things.

Think of it like a restaurant kitchen. The decisions are the recipes. The reusable parts are the prepared ingredients and the tools on the line. The agreements are how the kitchen runs: who orders stock, who changes the menu, how a new dish gets approved. A kitchen with great recipes but no process still serves inconsistent food on a busy night.

When a system is missing one of the three, you can usually spot it:

If you only have…What happens
DecisionsYou have a beautiful PDF of brand rules that nobody opens while they're working.
Reusable partsYou have a library, but it copies whatever inconsistency already existed, because nobody agreed on the rules first.
Decisions and parts, but no agreementsIt works brilliantly for a year. Then it drifts out of date, teams stop trusting it, and they start building their own versions again.

That last row is the most common failure we see. Which is why Layer One's first working rule is:

A design system is an agreement, not a library.Rule #1 — Layer One

01.3Style guide, UI kit, component library, design system

These four terms get used as if they mean the same thing. They don't, and mixing them up leads to real budget mistakes. Let's take them one at a time.

New wordComponentA reusable piece of interface, like a button, a text field or a dropdown, that's built once and used everywhere.

A style guide is a set of written rules about how the brand looks: the logo, colours, fonts, photography style and tone of voice. Think of the brand book your marketing agency handed over. It describes what things should look like, but it doesn't build anything.

A UI kit is a file in a design tool like Figma that contains ready-made pieces of interface (buttons, inputs, icons) that designers can drag into their screens. It makes designers faster and more consistent with each other. But engineers can't use it. They still have to rebuild everything in code by looking at the designs.

A component library is the same idea on the engineering side: buttons, inputs and menus written once in code, which engineers import into the product instead of writing their own. It makes engineers faster. But it often doesn't say when to use which piece, and it's frequently built separately from the designers' UI kit, so the two slowly drift apart.

A design system connects all of this. The designers' parts and the engineers' parts are the same parts, with the same names, built on the same underlying decisions, with guidance on how to use them and a team that keeps everything in sync.

A mistake we see often

"We have a design system" (it's a Figma file)

A team publishes a polished Figma library and announces a design system. Leadership relaxes; the consistency problem is solved. Six months later, engineering has built its own buttons anyway, because nothing they could actually use in code was ever delivered. A UI kit is a perfectly good first step. Just call it a UI kit, so nobody plans as if the code side is covered.

Which one do you have today?

Try this quick check. Every "no" shows you where your current setup stops.

  • Our colours, text sizes and spacing values have names (like "primary-blue" or "space-16"), not just hex codes copied around.
  • Engineers import buttons and inputs from a shared package instead of rebuilding them for each feature.
  • A designer and an engineer would use the same name for the same thing.
  • There's written guidance on when to use each piece, not just what it looks like.
  • Someone is responsible for keeping it up to date, and it's part of their actual job.
  • When something changes, people are told, and they can choose when to update.
  • People know how to ask for something new or suggest a change.

Seven yeses: you're running a design system. One to three: you have a UI kit or a component library, which is a fine place to be, as long as it's a deliberate stage and not where things got stuck.

01.4What's inside a complete design system

Now let's open the box. A complete design system has a few layers that stack on top of each other, plus some things that run through all of them. The important idea is that each layer is built from the one below it. That's what lets a change at the bottom ripple safely all the way up.

New wordDesign tokenA design decision with a name, like "primary-blue = #1C75D6". Design tools and code both read from the same list, so they always match.

Two of these layers deserve a plain-English introduction, because you'll meet them throughout the book.

Foundations are the basic visual decisions that everything else inherits: your colours, your text sizes, how much space goes between things, how pages are laid out. Change a foundation and you change everything built on it. Part 02 of this book is all about getting them right.

Tokens are how those decisions get written down so that both designers and engineers can use them. Instead of a designer writing "#1C75D6" on a spec and an engineer copying it into code (and maybe mistyping it), the colour gets a name, like color-primary. Design tools and code both read the value from the same place. If the colour ever changes, it changes in one place, and everywhere that uses the name updates.

The idea of building interfaces from small parts up to large ones was popularised by Brad Frost's Atomic Design,2 and the term "design tokens" came out of Salesforce's design system team.3 In October 2025 an industry working group published the first stable, shared standard for how tokens should be written,4 which tells you how mainstream the idea has become.

Complete doesn't mean big

A startup's complete design system might be a one-page list of principles, about a hundred tokens and fifteen components. It still has every layer, just a small amount of each. Completeness is about the layers being connected, not about how much is in them.

01.5How it connects design, engineering, product and business

Here's something that surprises most people: the biggest benefit of a design system isn't the components. It's that everyone ends up speaking the same language.

Without a system, a designer says "the blue button", a product manager says "the main CTA", and an engineer writes code for "btn-submit-v2". They're all talking about the same thing, and every handover is a small act of translation. Translations go wrong. With a system, there's one "primary button". The designer drags it in, the engineer types <Button variant="primary">, and both get exactly the same thing.

Here's what that looks like day to day, before and after:

WhoWithout a systemWith a working system
DesignersRedesign the same table, form and empty screen on every project. Spend hours writing handover specs.Start from known parts and spend their energy on the parts of the problem that are genuinely new.
EngineersBuild "yet another" dropdown. Fix the same keyboard bug in five places.Import a tested dropdown. Fix a bug once, and the fix reaches every screen on the next update.
Product managersEstimates swing wildly because nobody knows how much UI work is hiding in a feature.UI work is predictable, so conversations are about what the feature does, not how many pixels of padding it has.
The businessA rebrand takes quarters. Accessibility problems come back in every audit.Brand and accessibility changes are made in one place and rolled out.

01.6Why it matters more as you grow

A two-person team doesn't need a design system to stay consistent. They sit next to each other. So why does it suddenly become essential at thirty, sixty or three hundred people? Two simple reasons, and neither needs any industry statistics to understand.

Reason one: the number of conversations explodes

If every team that makes UI decisions has to stay in sync with every other team, the number of "have you talked to them?" conversations grows much faster than the number of teams. Four teams have six pairs that need to stay aligned. Sixteen teams have 120. This is the same arithmetic Fred Brooks described decades ago for software teams.5 If instead every team stays in sync with one shared system, sixteen teams need sixteen relationships, not 120.

Reason two: every change costs more

Remember the five buttons? Without a system, changing the brand colour means hunting down every place it was typed by hand: roughly products × platforms × places it appears. With a system, you change one value and release an update. The same goes for adding dark mode, fixing a contrast problem or refreshing your typography.

That's why the payoff of a design system usually shows up at the second product, the second platform or the first rebrand, not when the first button is built. At CARS24, for example, the work Layer One's founder led put more than ten products in three countries onto one shared colour and token system.1 Without a shared layer of named decisions, that kind of change would mean editing each product by hand.

Practice A simple test

Judge a design system by what it makes cheap

A good system makes the everyday thing fast (building a normal screen) and the scary thing cheap (changing a decision everywhere at once). If yours does neither, it's a catalogue, not a system.

Ten words you'll meet in this book

FoundationsThe basic visual decisions everything inherits: colour, text, spacing and layout.
TokenA design decision with a name, shared by design tools and code (space-16 = 16px).
ComponentA reusable piece of interface: a button, an input, a dialog.
VariantAn approved version of a component, like a primary or a secondary button.
PatternA proven way to solve a common problem using several components, such as how to show "no results found".
ThemeA complete set of values that changes the look everywhere at once, like dark mode or another brand.
LibraryThe place components live: a Figma library for designers, a code package for engineers.
AdoptionHow much of the real, shipped product is actually built with the system.
ContributionWhen someone outside the system team adds or improves something in the system.
ReleaseA new version of the system that teams can update to, with notes on what changed.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Inconsistency doesn't come from carelessness. It comes from many good people making reasonable decisions separately.
  2. A design system is decisions, reusable parts and working agreements. Missing any one of the three is the most common reason systems fail.
  3. A UI kit helps designers, a component library helps engineers, and a design system connects the two with shared names and a way to change.
  4. The value grows with size: more teams, more platforms and more change all make a shared system more valuable.

Chapter 02

02

Who needs a design system, and when

Here's a secret: every product already has a design system. It's just usually unwritten, inconsistent and living in a few people's heads. The real question isn't "do we need one?" It's "how much of it should we write down, and when?"

Read this if

You're trying to decide whether to invest now, later or not at all, or someone is telling you it's too early.

What you'll leave with
  1. Straight answers to the seven questions founders and leaders ask most.
  2. A simple way to tell where your company is today and what the next step looks like.
  3. A decision tree and a checklist you can bring to a planning meeting.

In this chapter

  1. 02.1The seven questions everyone asks
  2. 02.2Where are you today? A five-stage map
  3. 02.3A decision tree for your next planning meeting
  4. 02.4Signs you've outgrown what you have
  5. 02.5Four companies, four different answers
  6. 02.6Are you ready? A checklist

02.1The seven questions everyone asks

When we sit down with founders and product leaders, the same seven questions come up almost every time. Here are our honest answers, including when the answer would change.

Does every company need a design system?

Every company needs consistent design decisions. Not every company needs a formal system with its own team.

If your product has more than one screen, you've already made decisions about colours, text and spacing. The question is whether those decisions are written down and shared, or re-made by whoever builds the next screen. Two people sitting side by side can stay consistent just by talking. Once decisions are being made by people who don't talk every day, the unwritten system starts to split. Practice

Isn't this only for big enterprises?

No. Small companies run them too, just smaller.

zeroheight's 2025 survey of people who work on design systems found teams averaging about three people at companies with fewer than 100 employees, and about nine at companies with 500 or more.6 Documented (Keep in mind that people who answer a design systems survey usually have one.) What big companies need more of isn't system, it's coordination: more teams, more rules about who decides what. The core of a small system and a large one looks surprisingly similar.

Should a startup wait until it finds product–market fit?

Wait on the big system. Don't wait on the basics.

Before product–market fit, your product will change shape, so building a large custom component library is likely wasted effort. But naming your colours, text sizes and spacing takes days, not months, and it actually makes pivots cheaper: restyling a product built on named values is a quick change instead of a rebuild. Pair that with a good open-source component library (Radix, MUI and others) styled with your own values, and save custom components for when the product settles down. Practice

We have five or six designers. Is that enough to justify one?

Usually yes, but count engineers and products, not just designers.

Five designers on one product with eight engineers can stay consistent with a good UI kit and a shared list of named values. Five designers supporting forty engineers across a web app, a mobile app and an admin panel cannot. They'll spend half their week answering "which grey is it?" in Slack. What really drives the need is how many places UI is being built, and how far apart those places are. Practice

When is a UI kit enough?

When designers disagreeing with each other is the main problem, rather than design and code disagreeing.

A UI kit is often enough if you have one product, on one platform, built in one codebase, by fewer than about three squads, and engineering already uses a well-styled off-the-shelf component library. It stops designs drifting apart. It does nothing to stop code drifting away from design. When that second problem shows up, you've hit the ceiling.

How do we know we've outgrown what we have?

When inconsistency starts costing you time in delivery, not just debates in design reviews.

The checklist in 02.4 is a practical test. If you tick five or more items, you're already paying for a design system. You're just paying for it in rework instead of investment.

When is it too early, or unnecessary?

When nobody will own it, nobody will use it, or the product won't live long enough to benefit.

Hold off if you expect to rebuild your UI from scratch within six months; if one designer and one or two engineers build everything together; if it's a short-lived marketing site; or if engineering leadership hasn't agreed to use it. A system that only designers use is just an expensive UI kit. And be honest about ownership. A system nobody looks after decays faster than having no system at all, because people stop trusting it and start working around it.

02.2Where are you today? A five-stage map

Design systems grow in stages, like a staircase. The most useful thing you can do is figure out which step you're on and aim for the next one, not the top. Jumping straight to the top usually means building approval processes for components nobody uses yet.

StageYou'll recognise it when…The next stepWhat it takes
0 UnwrittenDesigners ask each other for hex codes; engineers measure screenshots.Write down the basics; publish a UI kit.1–3 weeks of one designer
1 Shared stylesThe designs look consistent, but the code is full of colours that "look about right".Name the values once and share them with code; build the most-used components.1–3 months, a designer and an engineer, part-time
2 Basics in codeNew screens use the package, older ones don't, and nobody owns incoming requests.Give it owners, documentation, releases and a way to contribute.A small dedicated team (1.5–3 people)
3 Looked afterSeveral teams contribute; updates ship on a rhythm; usage is tracked.Themes, multiple platforms, decision-making across the company.A dedicated team plus contributors in product teams
4 PlatformThe system is treated like infrastructure, with its own roadmap and targets.Keep it healthy; make change cheaper; automate checks.An ongoing product budget

These stages describe your company's relationship with its design system. Ben Callahan at Sparkbox describes a complementary maturity model for the system itself, which starts with "building version one" and then "growing adoption" before the system settles into a long-lived product.7 The two views fit together well. Whatever stage your company is at, the system goes through a hard early phase where it has to prove it's worth using. Chapter 05 covers that phase in detail.

02.3A decision tree for your next planning meeting

If you only have ten minutes with your leadership team, walk through these four questions. Notice that they ask about engineering and products before they ask about design. That's on purpose.

02.4Signs you've outgrown what you have

You don't need a consultant to tell you whether you have a consistency problem. Most of the evidence is sitting in your code and your calendar. Here's what to look for, and every item can be counted or observed, which is useful because these become your "before" numbers later.

In the code

  • A search for colour codes finds hundreds of different colours.
  • There's more than one button component (or dialog, or table) in the codebase.
  • The same accessibility bug has been fixed in several places.
  • Engineers think a brand colour change would take weeks, not hours.
  • Code reviews regularly turn into debates about spacing and styling.

In the organisation

  • Design review has become a bottleneck before every release.
  • New designers or engineers take weeks to learn "how we do UI here".
  • Customers or sales say your products feel like different companies.
  • A second product, platform, brand or acquisition is on the roadmap.
  • Enterprise customers now ask for accessibility compliance.
ScenarioThe dark mode request that exposed everything
The situation

A B2B product gets its most-requested feature for the third quarter running: dark mode. The PM estimates two sprints.

What goes wrong

Engineering finds 340 different colour values typed directly into the code, many of them nearly identical greys. There's no way to "switch" them, because nothing says which grey is for text and which is for borders. The estimate becomes two quarters.

What a design system changes

With colours named by their job ("text", "border", "background"), dark mode is a second set of values for the same names. It becomes a design task and a testing task, not a rewrite. Chapter 07 shows exactly how.

Practice How to read your score

0–2 ticks: you're fine for now; write down your basics. 3–5: you're paying for inconsistency in rework, so plan the next stage. 6 or more: not having a system is already costing you more than having one would. Start with an audit to see the size of the problem.

02.5Four companies, four different answers

To make this concrete, here are four situations we see again and again. They're composites, not real clients, but you'll probably recognise one of them. Illustrative

Company AA fintech startup: 3 designers, 4 engineers, still finding its feet

The founder has seen Stripe's design and wants "a proper design system". The product changes direction every month or two. Everyone sits in one room.

What they need

The basics only: about a week to name colours, text sizes and spacing, plus a good open-source component library styled to match.

Why not more?

Custom components would be redesigned with each pivot. The named values survive pivots; the components wouldn't.

When to revisit

When a second squad forms, or when they start building a mobile app.

Company BA Series B SaaS: 7 designers, 45 engineers, 2 products

They have their main web app and a recently acquired analytics product built with completely different code. There are three button styles in production, and customers keep asking for dark mode.

What they need

A two-week audit, then a shared set of named values that can style both products, and 15–20 shared components.

Who does it

A small core team of about two people, plus a named designer and engineer in each squad who contribute.

The payoff

Dark mode and visual consistency across both products, and a path to merge the acquired product's UI over time.

Company CAn enterprise with 30+ internal tools built by different vendors

Every tool looks different. Accessibility is now a legal requirement. Nobody owns the interface centrally, and each vendor uses its own technology.

What they need

Start with named values and accessibility rules, not components. Those can be added to old tools; new components can't be dropped into every old technology.

Who does it

A central team that sets the rules, with a clear process vendors must follow to contribute and get approval.

The payoff

A consistent, accessible baseline across tools, without rewriting them all at once.

Company DA marketing website, rebuilt every two or three years

The marketing team asks for "a design system for the website". An agency builds and maintains it.

What they need

A style guide and a set of reusable page sections in the CMS.

The smart move

Share the same named colours and fonts with the product, so the brand stays aligned between website and app.

What to avoid

Funding a product-grade system for a site that will be thrown away in two years.

02.6Are you ready? A checklist

Run through this before you commit budget. A "no" doesn't mean stop. It means that item becomes the first thing to work on.

  • A sponsor. A leader with budget who will defend the system in planning meetings.
  • Engineering on board. Engineering leadership agrees teams will use the shared code.
  • An owner. A named person with protected time, written into their role.
  • An audit. You know what exists today: styles, components, values, accessibility gaps.
  • A pilot team. One product team volunteers to build with it first.
  • "Before" numbers. You've counted the signs in 02.4, so you can show progress.
  • The right scope. You've picked the next stage, not the last one.
  • Known technology. You know which platforms and frameworks it has to support.

Audit before you build.Rule #2 — Layer One

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Every product has a design system; the choice is how much of it to write down and share.
  2. What drives the need is how many places UI gets built, more than how many designers you have.
  3. Before product–market fit, name your basic values and use an off-the-shelf library. Hold off on the big custom system.
  4. Aim for the next stage, not the final one, and don't start without engineering leadership on board.

Chapter 03

03

What a design system is worth

"It'll make us more consistent and efficient" won't get a budget approved. This chapter explains where the value really comes from, what has actually been measured, and how to measure it in your own company.

Read this if

You need to convince a CFO, a board or a sceptical engineering leader, or prove that your current system is earning its keep.

What you'll leave with
  1. The three ways a design system creates value, in plain terms.
  2. An honest view of the published evidence, including where it's weak.
  3. A short list of numbers you can start tracking this quarter.

In this chapter

  1. 03.1Three ways a design system saves you money
  2. 03.2What's actually been measured (and what hasn't)
  3. 03.3Nine outcomes, and why each one happens
  4. 03.4Numbers you can start tracking this quarter
  5. 03.5When the value shows up, and when it doesn't

03.1Three ways a design system saves you money

Every real benefit of a design system comes back to one of three simple ideas. If someone promises you a benefit that doesn't fit one of these, be a little suspicious.

01

Decide once

Teams stop re-deciding the same things: which grey, how much padding, how errors should look. That time goes to the problems that are actually new.

02

Build once

A component is built, tested and made accessible once, then reused everywhere. A bug fixed in it is fixed everywhere.

03

Change once

Because products point to shared parts instead of copies, changing the source changes every product. Rebrands, themes and accessibility fixes become updates, not projects.

Here's an everyday example of each.

Decide once. A designer starts a new settings page. Without a system, she spends the morning choosing toggle styles, spacing and section headings, then an hour in review defending those choices. With a system, those choices already exist. She spends the morning on what's actually hard: how to explain a confusing billing option to customers.

Build once. An engineer finds that dropdown menus can't be closed with the Escape key. Without a system, that bug exists in each team's own dropdown, so it gets fixed (or not) five separate times. With a system, it's fixed once and every team gets the fix with their next update.

Change once. Marketing refreshes the brand colour. Without a system, it's a project touching every product. With a system, it's one change and a release.

The first two save time steadily, a little every day. The third saves time in big lumps, whenever something changes, and over a product's life it's often the biggest saving of all. That's worth remembering when you build your business case: if you only count the first two, you're underselling the system.

03.2What's actually been measured (and what hasn't)

Let's be straight with you: the published research on design system value is thinner than the marketing suggests. Many of the impressive percentages you'll see online trace back to a handful of small studies, several run by companies that sell design tools. That doesn't mean the benefits aren't real. It means you should trust the mechanisms above, and measure the results in your own company rather than borrowing someone else's number.

Here are the three numbers worth knowing, along with how far to trust each one.

34%faster to complete a design task when designers had a relevant, up-to-date design system.Documented Figma's internal experiment.8 Run by a tool vendor, with limited detail on the sample.
47%faster to code a simple form using IBM's Carbon system than from scratch (2 hours vs 4.2).Documented Sparkbox.9 Only 8 developers, and they always built from scratch first.
79.1%of the world's top million home pages had text that was too low in contrast to read comfortably.Documented WebAIM Million 2025.10 A problem a design system can fix at the source.

Why mention the weaknesses? Because the first engineer who reads the Sparkbox study will notice that the developers built the form from scratch first, so by the second attempt they already understood the design. If your business case leans on that 47%, it falls over at the first question. If it leans on the mechanism ("we'll stop building dropdowns five times") plus your own measurements, it holds.

Two more findings help explain why consistency is a business issue, not a cosmetic one. A 1995 study by Kurosu and Kashimura found that people rated better-looking interfaces as easier to use, even when they weren't.11 And a 2003 Stanford study with more than 2,500 participants found that a website's overall look was the factor people mentioned most when judging whether they could trust it.12 Documented Neither study is about design systems specifically. But they show that a product which looks stitched together pays a real price in trust, and a design system is one of the most reliable ways to avoid looking stitched together.

A mistake we see often

Borrowing someone else's percentage

"Design systems make teams 47% faster" sounds great in a slide deck and collapses under one good question. Use published studies to show the idea is sound, then build your case on your own "before" numbers (see 03.4). Chapter 04 walks through a cautious way to do this.

03.3Nine outcomes, and why each one happens

When people say a design system "improves quality" or "speeds up delivery", it helps to know why, so you can explain it and later prove it. Here's each outcome with the reason behind it and something you can actually measure.

OutcomeWhy it happensHow you'd notice
Faster design workDesigners start from known parts and write fewer handover specs.Time from brief to ready-for-development design; fewer "how should this look?" questions.
Faster engineeringStandard UI is imported rather than rebuilt; less styling code to write and review.Shorter time to finish UI-heavy tickets; fewer review comments about styling.
Less duplicationOne version of each component instead of one per team.The number of different dropdowns (or tables, or dialogs) in your code goes down.
Higher qualityComponents are tested in every state; named values remove "close enough" colours.Fewer visual bugs per release; fewer one-off colour values in code.
AccessibilityContrast, keyboard use and screen-reader support are solved once in the system and inherited.Fewer automated accessibility errors; fewer findings in audits.
Easier maintenanceA fix or update in the system reaches every product through one update.Hours spent on a cross-product change, like a colour update.
Better collaborationDesign and engineering share one vocabulary.Fewer back-and-forth messages to clarify designs.
Faster launchesNew products and features start from a working kit instead of a blank page.Time from project start to first usable version of a new product.
More trustA coherent, polished product is seen as more usable and more credible.Customer survey answers about quality; sales feedback from demos.

Accessibility deserves its own line in the budget

Accessibility is where the business case has changed fastest in recent years. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 set out testable rules for things like text contrast, visible keyboard focus and the size of tap targets.13 Standard More and more regulation points to these rules. The European Accessibility Act, for example, applies to many digital products and services sold in the EU from 28 June 2025.14

A design system is the cheapest place to meet these rules. When the colour your whole product uses for body text is checked for contrast once, every screen passes. When the system's dialog handles keyboard focus properly, every dialog in every product does. Fixing accessibility screen by screen fixes it once, and only until the next screen gets built.

03.4Numbers you can start tracking this quarter

Layer One has a rule about this:

Measure time saved, not usage.Rule #8 — Layer One

Here's what we mean. It's tempting to report "our button has been used 12,000 times!" That tells you the system is being used. It doesn't tell you it's worth it. Track usage, by all means, because it's useful for the system team, but report outcomes to leadership.

You don't need fancy tooling to start. Most of these can be pulled with a few scripts and your existing project tracker.

What to trackIn plain wordsHow to get itHow often
AdoptionOf all the screens and files that show UI, what share use the system's components?A script that scans the code for imports from the system packageMonthly
Hard-coded valuesHow many colours and spacing values are typed directly into code instead of using names?A code search or lint rule that counts raw valuesMonthly
DuplicatesHow many different versions of the same component exist?Search the code for known component patternsQuarterly
Time to build UIHow long do UI tickets take, with and without the system?Your issue tracker, with UI tickets taggedQuarterly
Visual and accessibility bugsHow many design or accessibility bugs are found after development, per feature?Bug tracker labelsEach release
Cost of changeHow many hours did the last cross-product visual change take?Log the effort the next time it happensEach time
Request turnaroundHow long from someone asking for something to it being available?Your request boardQuarterly
SatisfactionDo designers and engineers agree that "the system makes my work faster"?A two-question surveyTwice a year

Practice The one thing to do first

Count before you build

Count your duplicates, hard-coded colours and accessibility errors before any system work ships. Without a starting point, every later number is just an opinion. With one, a single slide that says "different colours in our code: 412 → 61" does more for next year's budget than any industry statistic.

03.5When the value shows up, and when it doesn't

Design systems are a bit like planting a tree. There's a cost up front, the first year looks unimpressive, and the real payoff comes later. Knowing the shape of that curve helps you set honest expectations with leadership.

Four ways a design system can lose money

It's only fair to say that a badly run system can cost more than it saves. These are the four patterns we see most:

  • Nobody uses it. A system that only 10% of the product uses has nearly all the cost and almost none of the benefit. Adoption multiplies every outcome above.
  • It tries to do everything. A button with forty options is slower to use than just building the thing yourself.
  • It's a bottleneck. If every request waits weeks for the system team, product teams will work around it, and honestly, they'll be right to.
  • It stops changing. A system that doesn't keep up with the product becomes something teams fight against instead of something that helps them.

All four are problems of how the system is run, not of what's in it. That's what Chapter 05 is about.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Value comes from three things: deciding once, building once and changing once. The third is often the biggest.
  2. The published evidence is real but thin. Use it to show the idea works, not as your headline number.
  3. Count your "before" numbers now: duplicates, hard-coded values, accessibility errors.
  4. Report time and money saved to leadership, not how many times a button was used.

Chapter 04

04

The economics of design systems

"Isn't a design system a huge investment?" It can be, but it doesn't have to be. Spending on a design system works more like a volume knob than an on/off switch. This chapter shows you how to set the knob, and when to turn it up.

Read this if

You need a budget, a staffing plan or a return-on-investment argument, or someone has quoted you a frightening number and you want to know where it came from.

What you'll leave with
  1. The handful of things that make a design system cheap or expensive.
  2. Three realistic budgets, with every assumption out in the open.
  3. A simple, honest way to work out whether it pays off for you.

  2. 04.2What makes a design system cheap or expensive

04.1A quick word on the numbers

New wordFTE-monthOne person working full-time for one month. "6 FTE-months" could be one person for six months or three people for two.

Salaries vary enormously between countries and cities. A budget written in dollars for San Francisco means nothing in Bangalore, and the other way round. So in this chapter we count effort in FTE-months first, which works anywhere, and only then turn it into money using example monthly costs that you should swap for your own.

When we say "monthly cost per person", we mean the loaded cost: salary plus everything else a company pays for that person, such as benefits, equipment, office space and taxes. That's typically noticeably more than salary alone.

Illustrative Every figure in this chapter is an illustration

The numbers here come from clearly stated assumptions, not from measuring real projects. The method is the valuable part: change the assumptions to match your company and the answers change with them. The full model is in scripts/generate-data.mjs in this playbook's source files.

04.2What makes a design system cheap or expensive

When two companies get wildly different quotes for "a design system", the difference almost always comes down to the same few factors. The biggest two are platforms and technology: every extra platform (web, iPhone, Android) means building every component again, in a different language, by different engineers.

FactorCheaper when…More expensive when…Impact
PlatformsYou only build for the webYou build for web, iPhone and Android (and maybe desktop)Very high
TechnologyEveryone uses the same front-end frameworkSome teams use React, some Angular, some an old in-house stackVery high
Brands and themesOne brand, light mode onlyDark mode, several brands, or white-labelled versions for customersHigh
Existing messThe product is youngYears of inconsistent UI need to be moved overHigh
Number of components15–25 everyday components60+, including complex ones like data grids and chartsHigh
AccessibilityBuilt in from the startAdded afterwards to components that weren't designed for itMedium
DocumentationClear usage notes and code examplesA full public documentation site with tutorialsMedium
How spread out teams areOne office, one time zoneMany teams, outside agencies, many time zonesMedium
ToolingValues copied over by handAutomated pipelines, visual testing, automatic checksMedium (pays back)

This also explains why we always start with named values (tokens). They're the one part of the system that's written once and then automatically turned into code for every platform. A component has to be rebuilt per platform; a colour name doesn't.

04.3Who you need

A design system is built and run by a small mix of people. In a startup these might all be part-time hats worn by people with other jobs. In an enterprise they're full-time roles.

RoleWhat they actually doWhen you need it
System leadDecides what gets built next, keeps leadership on side, tracks whether teams are using it. Treats the system like a product.From Stage 2. Often half of a design or engineering lead's time.
System designerDesigns the foundations and components, keeps the Figma library tidy, writes usage guidance.From day one
System engineerBuilds components in code, sets up the pipeline that turns named values into code, publishes updates.From day one. This is the role most often missing.
Mobile engineersBuild the iPhone and Android versions of components from the same named values.When you have native apps
Accessibility specialistChecks components against the rules and tests with screen readers.Part-time from Stage 2
Writer / docsOrganises the documentation and writes guidance on wording and tone.Part-time from Stage 3
ContributorsDesigners and engineers in product teams who suggest and build improvements.From Stage 3, with time set aside in their team's plans

A mistake we see often

A design system team made only of designers

You end up with a beautiful Figma library and very little real-world use, because the product is built in code, not in Figma. As a rule of thumb, have at least as much engineering time on the core team as design time, and more once you support several platforms. Practice

04.4How long it takes

For a single web product, a first usable version usually takes four to six months, and the phases overlap. You don't wait for every colour to be perfect before starting on buttons. Here's what a typical first half-year looks like.

04.5Three realistic budgets

Here's what the first year might look like for three very different companies. Each budget is built from roles and months, then converted to money at three example monthly costs per person: $6,000, $12,000 and $20,000. Those are just example inputs to show the range. Use your own numbers. Illustrative

A few things jump out. The startup's system costs less than one engineer for a year, and that buys enough to stay consistent through its next funding round. The mid-sized company needs a small team of two or three people, not a department. And the enterprise budget is driven mostly by platforms: native iPhone and Android work alone is more than a fifth of it.

04.6A dedicated team, or your existing team?

This is one of the most common questions we get. The honest answer is "it depends on your size", so here's how to think about it.

Owned by an existing product teamA dedicated design system team
How it worksA designer and an engineer in a product team get protected time, often one or two days a week, to look after the system.A team whose whole job is the system, treating the product teams as its customers.
Good atCheap, and stays close to real product needs.Focus, quality, and serving many teams and platforms.
Watch out forDeadlines eat the protected time; the system quietly bends towards that one team's needs.Drifting away from real product work; becoming a bottleneck if others can't contribute.
Usually fitsOne product, fewer than about 30 engineers.Two or more products or platforms, roughly 40+ engineers.

For a reality check, zeroheight's 2025 survey found dedicated teams averaging about three people at companies under 100 employees, four at 100–499, and nine at 500 or more.6 Documented Even in very large companies, teams rarely grow past 20 to 25 people. At that size, the extra capacity comes from product teams contributing rather than from a bigger central team.

04.7The cost nobody budgets for: keeping it running

The most expensive budgeting mistake isn't overspending on the build. It's spending nothing after launch. Picture a team that builds a great system, celebrates the launch, and then gets reassigned to "real" product work. Within a year the components are behind what the products need, teams quietly make their own copies, and people stop using the system. All that investment slowly leaks away.

What "keeping it running" involves

  • Fixing bugs and accessibility problems in components
  • Adding new versions of components as products change
  • Upgrading when the underlying technology moves on
  • Keeping the Figma library tidy and in step with the code
  • Documentation, office hours and onboarding new people
  • Reviewing and accepting contributions from other teams
  • Checking whether teams are actually using it

Practice Plan for a team, not a percentage

People often ask, "what percentage of the build cost is maintenance?" We think that's the wrong question. Plan for the people who built the system to stay with it, at a similar or slightly smaller size, with their time shifting from building new things to helping teams use what exists. In our experience, systems whose builders move on right after launch rarely stay in use.

04.8Does it pay off? A simple way to work it out

Return on investment (ROI) sounds like finance jargon, but the idea is simple: is the time and money the system saves bigger than what it costs? There are three pieces to add up.

  1. Time saved from reuse

    How many people build UI, how much of their time goes on UI, how much of that work the system covers, and how much faster it makes them. Multiply those together to get hours, then multiply by an hourly cost.

  2. Big changes made cheaper

    For each planned change, like a rebrand, dark mode or an accessibility clean-up, estimate the cost with and without a system. Only count changes that are actually on the roadmap.

  3. What the system costs

    The system team's cost for the year.

// The same thing, written as a formula
hours_saved = people × working_hours × share_of_time_on_UI × adoption × speed_up
value       = hours_saved × hourly_cost + savings_from_planned_big_changes
ROI         = (value − system_cost) ÷ system_cost

A worked example: Ledgerly

Ledgerly is the fictional finance product we use throughout this book. It has 40 engineers and 6 designers. We'll assume the system makes work it covers 20% faster. That's deliberately well below the 34% and 47% from Chapter 03, because those came from best-case tasks. We'll let adoption grow over three years, and we'll count only time saved from reuse, ignoring every big change, to see the most cautious picture.

We'll admit that's not the flashy answer people expect, and we think that's exactly why it's useful. It shows that at 40 engineers, a two-person team doesn't pay for itself on speed alone in year one. The case depends on two things: getting teams to adopt the system quickly, and the big changes that are coming. That tells you exactly where to focus.

04.9Start small, and earn the next step

You don't have to commit to the whole thing up front. The approach we recommend is to fund the system one step at a time, and let each step earn the next. Each step has a clear "gate": something you can point to that justifies the next round of investment.

  1. Audit — two weeks

    Find out what you have in design and code, and count your duplicates, hard-coded values and accessibility problems. Gate: leadership agrees on the top problems.

  2. Foundations and named values — one to two months, part-time

    Colours, text, spacing and layout, named and shared by design and code. Gate: one product team ships new work using only the named values.

  3. The ten most-used components — two to three months

    Pick them by how often they appear in your audit, not by which ones are fun to design. Gate: the pilot team is measurably faster, or has fewer UI bugs.

  4. Documentation, releases and contribution — ongoing

    Make it usable by people who didn't build it. Gate: a second team adopts it without hand-holding, and someone outside the core team contributes something.

  5. Scale up — themes, platforms, governance

    Only now invest in multiple brands, native platforms and formal decision-making. Gate: most new work uses the system, and there's a real upcoming change that needs it.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Cost is driven mostly by platforms, technology and brands. Named values are the cheapest part and pay back first.
  2. Staff the system with engineers as well as designers, and keep the team after launch.
  3. Be honest in your ROI: on speed alone, payback takes time; adoption and big upcoming changes make the case.
  4. Fund it in steps, and let each step earn the next.

Up next →Chapter 05: Running a design system day to day

Chapter 05

05

Running a design system day to day

Building a design system is the easy part. Running it is where most of them succeed or fail. Who owns it? Who decides what goes in? What happens when two teams want different things, or an update breaks someone's screen? This chapter is about the everyday operation.

Read this if

You're setting up a system team, your system isn't being used as much as you hoped, or product teams have started calling the system team "the bottleneck".

What you'll leave with
  1. A clear picture of the ways companies organise design system ownership, and which fits you.
  2. A practical process for requests, contributions, updates and breaking changes.
  3. Ways to get people using the system, and to keep it healthy for years.

In this chapter

  1. 05.1It's a product, not a project
  2. 05.2Who owns it? Four ways to organise
  3. 05.3Who decides what goes in?
  4. 05.4From "we need this" to "it's in the system"
  5. 05.5Contributions: letting product teams help
  6. 05.6Shipping changes without breaking anything
  7. 05.7Getting people to actually use it
  8. 05.8Keeping it healthy for years

05.1It's a product, not a project

A project has an end date. You build it, you launch it, you move on. A lot of design systems are treated this way, and that's exactly why they fail. Nathan Curtis, one of the most influential voices in the field, put it in a phrase that has stuck for a decade: a design system isn't a project, it's a product, serving products.15

What does "product" mean in practice? It means the system has users, who are the designers and engineers in your product teams. It has a roadmap of what's coming next. It ships updates on a regular rhythm. It offers support when people get stuck. And somebody checks whether it's actually working for the people who use it. Ben Callahan of Sparkbox describes the people who build with a system as its "subscribers", and that's a useful way to think about them. They chose to rely on you. Keep earning it.7

Product habitWhat it looks like for a design system
Know your usersRegularly sit with product teams. Look at what they build outside the system, and ask why.
Keep a roadmapA public list of what's coming, ordered by how many teams need it and how painful the gap is.
Ship on a rhythmRegular updates with clear notes on what changed, so teams can plan.
Offer supportA Slack channel with someone answering, weekly office hours, and a short onboarding session for new joiners.
Measure what mattersIs it being used? Is it saving time? Do people like working with it? (See 05.8.)

Practice A simple test

Ask a designer in a product team: "If the system doesn't have what you need, what do you do?" If they can answer confidently, you have an operating model. If they shrug and say "I just make my own", you have a library.

05.2Who owns it? Four ways to organise

Every company that runs a design system has to answer one question early: whose job is it? In his 2015 essay on team models, Nathan Curtis described the options that most of the industry still uses today.16 Here they are, in plain terms.

One team's system (Curtis calls it "solitary"). One product team builds a system for itself, and others borrow it. It's fast and grounded in real work, but it naturally bends towards that one team's needs, so other teams often don't adopt it.

A central team ("centralised"). A dedicated team builds and runs the system for everyone. Quality and focus are high, but the team can drift away from what products actually need, and it can become a queue everyone is stuck in.

Shared ownership ("federated"). Designers and engineers across product teams share the work, with no central team. It sounds fair and efficient. In practice it's often nobody's real job, so it quietly stalls. Curtis himself later concluded that successful systems always have a central team, and also seek participation from a wider community.17

Central team plus contributors (a hybrid). A core team owns quality and direction, and product teams contribute improvements back. Salesforce described their version as "cyclical": the core and the contributors constantly feed each other.18 This is where most mature systems end up.

Real-world exampleSpotify: from 22 systems to one family
What happened

After Spotify's original central design system team was disbanded, teams started building their own. By the time the company looked again, it had 22 separate design systems.

The problem

Each one made sense locally, but together they made the product inconsistent and duplicated a lot of work.

What they did

They created Encore, a "system of systems": shared foundations at the core, with local systems for specific products or platforms on top.19

Practice Our recommendation

Start with one team or a central team while you get the basics right. As soon as two or more teams depend on the system, move to "central team plus contributors", and do it on purpose: set aside contributor time in product teams' plans instead of hoping people will help in their spare time.

05.3Who decides what goes in?

Imagine two product teams. The payments team needs a date picker that shows bank holidays. The reporting team needs a date picker that selects ranges of months. Both ask the system team for "a date picker". Who decides what gets built, and does it go into the shared system at all?

This is the everyday reality of running a system, and the answer starts with a simple idea: not everything belongs in the core.

In our date picker example, the system team builds (or improves) a basic, accessible date picker in the core. The reporting team builds a month-range picker as an extension, using core parts. The payments team adds bank holidays locally. Everyone gets what they need, the core stays clean, and if a third team later needs month ranges, the extension is a strong candidate to move into the core.

Write down who decides what

Most arguments about design systems are really arguments about who gets to decide. You can prevent most of them by writing it down in advance. Here's a starting point for a central team with contributors:

DecisionWho makes the callWho should be asked first
Changing a foundation (colours, text sizes)System leadProduct designers, brand, engineering
Adding a new component to the coreSystem leadThe teams that asked for it
Adding a variation to an existing componentSystem designerThe requesting team
How a component works in code, and changes that would break thingsSystem engineersProduct engineers
Whether a component meets accessibility rulesSystem lead (with an accessibility specialist)—
Building a local, product-only componentThe product teamSystem designer (a quick heads-up)
Removing an old componentSystem leadEvery team still using it
The system's roadmap and budgetDesign and engineering leadershipSystem lead, product teams

Look at the sixth row. Product teams are allowed to build their own components when the system doesn't cover what they need. A healthy system doesn't forbid that. It just asks teams to say so, so the system can learn from it.

05.4From "we need this" to "it's in the system"

Let's follow a real request through the system. Priya is a product designer on the billing team. She's designing a new invoice screen and needs a way to show a short list of key facts: amount, due date, status. Nothing in the system quite fits.

What happens next decides whether Priya trusts the system or quietly gives up on it. Brad Frost has described a governance process that many teams use as a starting point,22 and here's our version of it, in plain steps.

  1. Check the system first

    Priya searches the system and its documentation. If something fits, she uses it. Done.

  2. Talk to the system team early

    Nothing fits, so she posts in the system's Slack channel with a screenshot and a sentence about the problem. Not a finished design, just the need. Early is cheap; late is expensive.

  3. Decide: one-off or shared?

    The system designer replies within a day or two. Have other teams needed this? It turns out the subscriptions team built something very similar last month. Two teams need it, so it's a candidate for the system.

  4. Agree what "good" looks like

    They agree on a rough scope together: which states it needs, how it behaves on small screens, and accessibility requirements.

  5. Build it once, properly

    Either the system team builds it, or Priya's team builds it with the system team's help (that's a contribution; see 05.5). Either way it gets designed for every state, built in code, tested and documented.

  6. Review, release and announce

    A final check, then it ships in the next update with a short note: what it is, when to use it, and a thank-you to Priya's team.

  7. Teams pick it up

    Billing and subscriptions both update and use the shared version. The subscriptions team's one-off copy is retired.

Meanwhile, Priya doesn't wait. If her deadline is before step 6, she builds a local version from system parts and swaps it for the official one later. The system should never be the reason a product team misses a deadline.

How do you decide what makes the cut?

The UK government's GOV.UK Design System publishes its criteria openly, and they're a great model. To be accepted, a proposed component or pattern must be useful (there's evidence other teams need it) and unique (it doesn't duplicate something that exists). Before it's published, it's checked to be usable (tested with real users, including disabled users), consistent (built from existing styles and parts) and versatile (works across browsers, devices and assistive technology).23 Documented You can adopt those five words almost as they are.

Practice The rule of two

Our simplest test: something goes into the core when at least two teams need it. Until then, it lives locally with the team that built it, made from system parts so it's easy to promote later. This keeps the core free of one-offs and gives the system a steady supply of tried-and-tested candidates.

05.5Contributions: letting product teams help

A central team of three can't keep up with the needs of fifteen product teams. Contribution, meaning product teams improving the system themselves, is how small system teams serve big organisations. But it only works if contributing is easy and the effort matches the size of the change.

Nathan Curtis makes a useful distinction between small and large contributions.24 Small ones are things like fixing a bug, improving an accessibility issue or correcting documentation: changes that are clearly improvements, which should go through a normal, quick review. Large ones change how something works or add something new, and they deserve a proper proposal and discussion before anyone builds them.

ScenarioThe engineer who fixed a bug and never contributed again
The situation

Arjun, a product engineer, finds that the system's dropdown can't be closed with the Escape key. He fixes it in an afternoon and submits the change.

What goes wrong

The change sits for three weeks waiting for a design review and a "contribution committee" meeting. By the time it's merged, Arjun has worked around it in his own code. He doesn't bother next time.

What should happen

A clear bug fix is a small contribution: one engineer reviews it within a few days, it ships in the next patch, and Arjun gets a thank-you in the release notes.

Proposals for bigger changes

New wordRFC"Request for comments": a short written proposal shared for feedback before a big decision is made.

For larger changes, many teams use a short written proposal, often called an RFC. Keep it to a page: what problem are we solving, what are the options, what do we recommend, and what would teams have to change? Share it for comments for a fixed time, say a week, and then the person responsible decides. Written proposals sound bureaucratic, but they're actually faster than meetings, because people can comment when it suits them and the reasoning is saved for later.

One last thought from Curtis that's worth holding on to: he has said he dislikes the word "contribution" because it makes teams focus on the output (a pull request) instead of the outcome (a better system for everyone).25 The point isn't to collect contributions. It's to make the system better and to make product teams feel it's theirs.

05.6Shipping changes without breaking anything

Here's a situation that happens in almost every design system eventually. The system team decides buttons should have slightly more rounded corners and a little more padding. It's a small visual tweak. They ship it on a Friday. On Monday, three product teams report broken screens: buttons no longer fit in a table row, a toolbar wraps onto two lines, and a checkout button now pushes the price off the screen on small phones.

Nothing in the code "broke". But the products did. Nathan Curtis wrote a whole article about exactly this: changes to colour, size and spacing can break a product as surely as a change to the code.26

Version numbers, in plain words

New wordBreaking changeAn update that could make something stop working or look wrong in a product, so teams need to check or change their own work.

Most systems label their updates with a three-part version number, like 4.2.1, following a widely used convention called semantic versioning.27 It's simpler than it sounds. Each number tells teams how careful they need to be when updating:

Which number changesWhat it means for teamsDesign system examples
First (4 → 5)"Careful: you'll need to check or change your work."A component renamed or removed; a named colour removed; button sizes changed in a way that affects layouts.
Middle (4.2 → 4.3)"New things added; nothing you use should change."A new component, a new variation, a new icon.
Last (4.2.1 → 4.2.2)"Fixes only. Safe to update."A bug fix; an accessibility fix that doesn't change size or layout; a docs correction.

Curtis's series on releasing design systems goes into this in depth: how often to release, how to number versions, and how to handle breaking changes.28 The headline advice is simple. Decide in advance which kinds of visual change count as breaking, write it down, and stick to it. In our button story, a change to padding that affects layouts should have been a "first number" release, announced in advance, with screenshots and a test period.

Retiring old things gracefully

New wordDeprecationMarking something as "old, please stop using it" before actually removing it, so teams have time to switch.

Sooner or later you'll need to replace a component. Doing it suddenly breaks things; never doing it leaves a mess. The healthy middle path looks like this. First, mark the old component as deprecated: it still works, but the documentation and a warning in the code say "please use the new one". Then give teams a guide to switching, and, where the change is mechanical, an automated script to do it for them. Track who's still using the old version. Only remove it in the next "first number" release, after a notice period everyone knows about in advance.

Telling people what changed

Release notes are the system's most-read documentation, so write them for the people using the system, not for the people who built it. Compare "Refactored Button padding tokens" with "Buttons are now 4px taller. If you've placed buttons inside table rows, check they still fit." The second one actually helps someone. Add before-and-after screenshots for anything visual. For bigger releases, a ten-minute demo in a team meeting goes a long way.

05.7Getting people to actually use it

Here's an uncomfortable truth: a design system nobody uses is just an expensive side project. Adoption is the system team's most important job, and Ben Callahan's maturity model puts "growing adoption" right after "building version one" for good reason.7 It's the stage where many systems stall.

The good news is that adoption is rarely about persuasion. It's about making the system the easiest way to get work done. Teams take the path of least resistance. Your job is to make sure that path runs through the system.

Start with a pilot

Dan Mall, in his book Design That Scales, recommends building the system through pilots: real product projects where the system is used, tested and improved at the same time as the product work gets done.29 Like a TV pilot, it's a low-risk way to find out what works before you roll it out widely. It also gives you your first success story: a real team that shipped faster, which is far more convincing than any slide.

Scenario"I couldn't find it, so I made my own"
The situation

A new designer joins and needs a warning banner. The Figma library has 400 components with names like "Alert_v2_final" and "Banner/New/Warning (old)".

What goes wrong

She can't tell which one is current, so she draws her own. Engineering builds it from scratch. The product now has a fourth kind of warning.

What fixes it

Clear names, removing or hiding old versions, a search-friendly description on every component, and a "start here" page. Findability is adoption. Part 03 covers library organisation in detail.

What works

Great documentation

Teams use what they can understand in five minutes before a deadline. Layer One's rule: docs decide adoption.

Champions in each team

One designer and one engineer per product team who get early previews and a direct line to the system team.

Office hours

A weekly slot where anyone can bring a screen and get help building it with the system.

Starter templates

New projects begin with the system already set up, so using it is the default, not an extra step.

Automatic nudges

Code checks that flag hard-coded colours or old components during code review.

Share the credit

Celebrate contributors and pilot teams in release notes and all-hands meetings.

A mistake we see often

Mandating adoption before earning it

"From next quarter, all teams must use the design system." If the system isn't ready to cover their needs, teams will comply on paper and work around it in practice, and they'll resent it. Make it genuinely useful first; mandates work best when they confirm something teams already want.

05.8Keeping it healthy for years

Design systems rarely die suddenly. They fade. Updates get less frequent, requests pile up, the Figma library and the code drift apart, and one day someone says "we should build a new design system", and the cycle starts again.

You can see it coming if you check a few simple signals regularly. Review them with the team monthly, and with leadership every quarter. Look at which way they're moving, not at hitting exact targets.

SignalWhat to look atHealthyWarning sign
UsageShare of UI built with the system; how many products are on a recent versionRising; most products within one major versionFlat; products stuck on old versions
CoverageHard-coded values in code; local components per productHard-coded values fallingLocal components growing faster than the core
QualityOpen bugs; accessibility errorsBugs fixed faster than they arriveThe same kind of bug keeps coming back
SpeedTime from request to release; number of contributionsDays to weeks; contributions growingMonths; contributions dropping to zero
Feeling"The system makes my work faster" (% who agree)Most agree, and risingPeople call it a blocker

Tidy as you go

New wordDesign debtShortcuts and inconsistencies that pile up over time and make future work slower, like clutter in a garage.

Every system builds up clutter: components that no longer quite fit, workarounds that became permanent, copies that teams made and modified, old versions still in use, and places where the Figma library and the code no longer match. That's normal. The problem is clutter nobody can see. Keep a simple, visible list of it (a "debt register"), and set aside a fixed slice of every cycle, around a fifth of the team's time, to clear some of it. Practice Teams that tidy a little all the time rarely need a big rewrite.

Watch your own capacity

Finally, look after the team. In zeroheight's 2025 survey, 41% of respondents said they didn't have enough people to run their system, and that was most common at smaller companies.6 Documented An overstretched system team becomes slow, a slow team becomes a bottleneck, and a bottleneck gets worked around. Protecting the team's capacity is part of protecting the system.

Operating checklist

  • Ownership model chosen and written down
  • Who-decides-what table agreed (05.3)
  • A clear path from request to release (05.4)
  • Contribution levels published, with quick reviews for small fixes
  • Core, extensions and local levels defined
  • Versioning rules, including which visual changes are "breaking"
  • A deprecation process with a notice period
  • Release notes written for the people using the system
  • A pilot team and champions in each product team
  • A monthly health check and a visible debt list

Leave the team able to run it without us.Rule #10 — Layer One

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Treat the system as a product with users, a roadmap, releases and support, not a project with an end date.
  2. Most mature systems end up with a central team plus contributors from product teams. Plan contributor time on purpose.
  3. Not everything belongs in the core. Use levels (core, extensions, local) and the rule of two.
  4. Decide in advance which visual changes count as breaking, and announce changes in plain language.
  5. Adoption is the main job: pilot, document well, and make the system the easiest path.

Building the foundations of a design system

Colour, text, spacing and layout are the decisions every button and every screen inherits. Get them right and everything built on top gets easier. Get them wrong and every component carries the mistake. This part walks through each one, step by step, and shows how a decision becomes working code.
