13

Deciding what to build first

The most common way to waste the first six months of a design system is to start with the components that are fun to design instead of the ones teams actually need. This chapter shows how to find out what you have, decide what matters, and say "not yet" to the rest.

Read this if

You're planning which components to build, deciding between building your own and using an open-source library, or drowning in requests.

What you'll leave with
  1. A step-by-step way to take stock of the interface you already have.
  2. A simple way to rank what to build first.
  3. A realistic first-year plan, and the confidence to say "not yet".

In this chapter

  1. 13.1Start with what you already have
  2. 13.2Count what matters
  3. 13.3Rank it: what to build first
  4. 13.4Build, borrow or buy?
  5. 13.5Saying "no" and "not yet"
  6. 13.6A realistic first year

13.1Start with what you already have

Before you design anything new, find out what already exists. Brad Frost calls this an interface inventory: you go through your product, screenshot every distinct version of every interface element, and group them by type.59 In his original write-up he describes screenshotting the buttons from just a few pages of a bank's website and finding a startling variety of styles. That's typical. Every product we've audited has been the same.

Scenario"We have one date picker." (They had three.)
The situation

Ledgerly's team believes their product is fairly consistent. They spend two afternoons doing an inventory before starting their design system.

What they find

7 kinds of primary button, 3 date pickers (one from an old library, two custom), 4 different "something went wrong" messages, 11 shades of border grey, and 2 tables that sort differently.

Why it matters

Now they know where the pain is, they have "before" numbers to show progress, and leadership can see the problem on one wall. The inventory became the business case.

How to run an inventory in a week

  1. Pick your scope

    Your top 15–25 screens by traffic or importance, across every product and platform. You don't need every screen to see the pattern.

  2. Screenshot by category

    Buttons, form fields, menus, messages, tables, cards, navigation, icons, colours, text styles. One slide or board per category.

  3. Group the near-duplicates

    Put things that are meant to be the same next to each other. The differences will jump out.

  4. Check the code too

    Ask engineers to count how many different implementations exist for the main components, and how many raw colour values are in the code.

  5. Show it to people

    Walk leadership and product teams through the boards. It's the fastest way to build shared understanding of the problem.

Practice Do it together

Run the inventory as a team exercise with designers and engineers, not as a solo audit. People who find the seven buttons themselves become supporters of the system. People who are shown a report about their seven buttons become defensive.

13.2Count what matters

An inventory tells you what exists. To decide what to build first, you need two more pieces of information for each component: how often it's used and how much trouble it's causing today.

How often is the easy one. Engineers can count how many times each kind of component appears in the code, and designers can count in their design files. Trouble is a bit more judgement: how many different versions are there, how many bugs and accessibility problems have been reported, and how much time do teams spend rebuilding or debating it?

Notice something about the chart: the components with the most versions are usually the most common ones. That's not a coincidence. The more often something is built, the more chances there are for it to drift. Which is good news, because it means fixing a small number of everyday components fixes a large share of the inconsistency.

13.3Rank it: what to build first

Put your two pieces of information together and you get a simple map. Plot each component by how often it's used and how much trouble it causes today.

This is less exciting than designing a fancy data visualisation component, and that's exactly the point. The boring components are where the most time is wasted and the most inconsistency lives. Nathan Curtis suggests a similar exercise for teams starting a system, which he calls "picking parts, products and people": agree on the ten most important parts, the products that will use them first, and the people who'll do the work.60

A mistake we see often

Starting with the hardest component

A team decides to begin with the data table "because it's the biggest problem". Six months later they have a sophisticated table, nothing else, and product teams have stopped waiting. Start with components you can finish in days, so teams see progress quickly, and tackle the big ones once you have momentum and a working process.

13.4Build, borrow or buy?

You don't have to build every component from scratch. There are excellent open-source libraries, and one kind in particular is worth knowing about.

New wordHeadless componentA component that handles behaviour (keyboard use, focus, accessibility) but has no visual style, so you can apply your own.

Headless libraries, such as Radix, provide components that work correctly (keyboard navigation, focus handling, screen-reader support) but come without any visual styling. You add your own look using your foundations. It's a bit like buying a well-engineered car chassis and designing your own body for it. Building accessible behaviour for complex components like menus, dialogs and comboboxes is genuinely hard; the W3C's own guide to these patterns runs to dozens of pages.61 Borrowing tested behaviour can save months.

ApproachGood forWatch out for
Build your ownFull control; exactly your needs; no outside dependency.Slowest. Accessible behaviour for complex components is hard to get right.
Headless library + your stylesCorrect, accessible behaviour out of the box; your own look; much faster.You depend on the library's updates and its way of doing things.
Fully styled library (themed)Fastest to start; great for early-stage products and internal tools.Hard to make it look truly yours; heavy theming can be harder than building.

Practice What we usually recommend

For most product companies: build simple components yourself (buttons, badges, cards), because they're easy and you'll want full control. Use a headless library for complex interactive ones (menus, dialogs, comboboxes, date pickers), because the behaviour is the hard part. Use a fully styled library only before product–market fit, or for internal tools where brand matters less.

13.5Saying "no" and "not yet"

Once a design system exists, requests arrive constantly. "Can we have a special pricing card?" "Can the button have a gradient for the campaign page?" "We need a timeline component." A system team that says yes to everything ends up with a bloated, inconsistent library, which is exactly the problem it was created to solve.

Saying no doesn't mean refusing to help. It usually means one of three answers:

"Use this instead"

It already exists

Often an existing component, or a combination of them, already solves the problem. Showing how is a quick win for everyone.

"Build it locally"

It's a one-off

If only one team needs it, they build it from system parts and own it. If a second team needs it later, it becomes a candidate for the core.

"Yes, next quarter"

It's real but not urgent

It goes on the public roadmap with an honest timeline, so the team can plan around it.

This is the rule of two from Chapter 05 in action: something enters the core when at least two teams need it. Brad Frost describes product-specific combinations that stay outside the core as "recipes",21 and Nathan Curtis describes the same idea as tiers below a high-quality core.20 Whatever you call it, having a respectable place for "not in the core" components is what makes it possible to say no without being unhelpful.

13.6A realistic first year

Here's how Ledgerly might plan its first year, using everything in this chapter. Notice that each quarter delivers something teams can use straight away, and that the work is always tied to a real product project, a pilot, rather than built in isolation. Dan Mall argues that pilots are the best way to start and sustain a design system, because they keep the system honest about real needs.29

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Start with an interface inventory, done together with designers and engineers.
  2. Rank components by how often they're used and how much trouble they cause. The boring everyday ones usually win.
  3. Borrow tested behaviour for complex components; build simple ones yourself.
  4. Have a respectable home for "not in the core" components, so you can say "not yet" without being unhelpful.

Up next →Chapter 14: Designing a component that lasts

Chapter 14

14

Designing a component that lasts

A component in a design system is used in hundreds of places by people you'll never meet, with content you'll never see. Designing one is less about making it look good in a mock-up and more about predicting everything that will happen to it in real life.

Read this if

You design components, review them, or keep finding that system components break when real content and real people get hold of them.

What you'll leave with
  1. A process that starts from real use, not from a blank canvas.
  2. Checklists for states, edge cases and accessibility.
  3. A clear "ready to build" standard for handing a component to engineering.

In this chapter

  1. 14.1Start from real use, not a blank canvas
  2. 14.2Design every state and every edge
  3. 14.3Accessible from the start
  4. 14.4The words are part of the component
  5. 14.5"Ready to build": what a finished design includes
  6. 14.6Test it in the real product

14.1Start from real use, not a blank canvas

When designers start a new component, the instinct is to open a blank frame and design the ideal version. For a system component, that's the wrong starting point. The right one is the inventory from Chapter 13: every version of this component that already exists, and every situation it's used in.

ScenarioThe alert that looked perfect until it met real messages
The situation

A designer creates a beautiful alert component. In the mock-up, every message is one short line: "Changes saved."

What goes wrong

In the real product, messages include "Your payment of ₹1,24,000 to Acme Supplies could not be processed because the bank declined the transaction. Try another payment method." The alert wraps onto four lines, the icon floats in the middle, and the close button overlaps the text.

What would have helped

Collecting twenty real alert messages from the product before designing, and testing the design with the longest, shortest and strangest ones.

So before you design, gather the evidence:

  • Every existing version of the component, from the inventory, and what each one was trying to do.
  • Real content: actual labels, messages and data from the product, including the longest and the oddest.
  • Where it's used: in a table, in a dialog, on a phone, in a dense dashboard, in a marketing page.
  • What teams have asked for: open requests and complaints about the current versions.
  • How others do it: look at how mature public systems handle the same component, for ideas and pitfalls.

14.2Design every state and every edge

In Chapter 12 we saw a text field in eight states. Most components have more situations than people expect, and the ones you forget are the ones that end up looking broken in production. Here's a checklist we use for every component.

SituationQuestions to answer
Interaction statesDefault, hover, pressed, keyboard focus, selected, disabled, read-only. What does each look like?
Data statesEmpty, loading, partly loaded, error, success. What shows while we wait? What if there's nothing to show?
Too much contentA very long name, a huge number, 300 items in a list. Does it wrap, cut off with "…", or scroll?
Too little contentA one-character name, a single item. Does it still look intentional?
Other languagesSome languages need much more space than English for the same message; some read right to left. Does the layout survive?
Screen sizesWhat happens on a phone? In a narrow side panel? On a very wide screen?
Bigger text and zoomIf someone sets their text size larger, or zooms to 200%, does anything get cut off?
CombinationsError and disabled? Loading and selected? Which combinations are possible, and which should be prevented?

Practice The "stress test" frame

Keep a page in your design file next to every component called "stress test". Put the component in it with the longest real content, the shortest, an empty state, an error, a translated version and a phone-width version. Review that page, not the pretty one. It takes an hour and saves weeks of bug reports.

14.3Accessible from the start

Layer One's fifth rule is accessible by default, not by audit. For components, this matters even more than anywhere else, because every accessibility problem in a component is copied into every screen that uses it. The good news is that the reverse is also true: get a component right once, and every screen gets it right.

Accessibility can sound intimidating, so here it is in plain terms. For each component, make sure that:

Everyone can…Which meansSource
See itText has enough contrast (4.5:1), and so do the edges of fields and buttons (3:1). Information never relies on colour alone.Standard WCAG 1.4.3, 1.4.11, 1.4.113
Use it with a keyboardEvery action can be reached with Tab and triggered with Enter or Space. Menus and dialogs follow the standard keyboard patterns.Standard WCAG 2.1.1; ARIA patterns61
See where they areA clear focus outline appears when moving with the keyboard.Standard WCAG 2.4.7
Hear what it isScreen readers announce what it is ("button"), its name ("Send invoice") and its state ("expanded", "selected").Standard WCAG 4.1.2
Hit itClick and tap targets are at least 24 × 24px, and 44–48 on touchscreens.Standard WCAG 2.5.854
Understand errorsError messages say what's wrong and how to fix it, and are connected to the field they describe.Standard WCAG 3.3.1, 3.3.3
Avoid discomfortAnimations respect the "reduce motion" setting on people's devices.Practice

For complex interactive components like menus, tabs, dialogs and comboboxes, don't invent the keyboard behaviour. The W3C's ARIA Authoring Practices Guide documents the expected behaviour for each of these patterns, including which keys do what, and it's the reference most accessible component libraries follow.61 Documented

ScenarioThe dialog you couldn't escape
The situation

A team builds its own confirmation dialog. It looks great and works perfectly with a mouse.

What goes wrong

Keyboard users press Tab and the focus goes behind the dialog into the page. Escape doesn't close it. Screen readers don't announce it. It ships in 40 places before anyone notices.

The system fix

One dialog component with focus kept inside, Escape to close, focus returned afterwards, and a proper announcement. Fixed once; every one of the 40 dialogs inherits it.

14.4The words are part of the component

A button isn't finished when its colour and padding are decided. What it says matters just as much. Good systems include writing guidance alongside each component, because consistent words are as important as consistent pixels.

ComponentInstead of…Write…Why
Button"Submit", "OK", "Yes""Send invoice", "Delete 3 files"Say what will happen. People often read only the button.
Error message"Invalid input""Enter a date after 1 January 2026"Say what's wrong and how to fix it.
Empty state"No data""No invoices yet. Create your first invoice to get paid faster."Explain why it's empty and what to do next.
Confirmation"Are you sure?""Delete this customer? Their 12 invoices will also be deleted."Spell out the consequence.
LabelPlaceholder text onlyA visible label above the fieldPlaceholders disappear when you type, and are often low-contrast.

You don't need a full content style guide on day one. Start with one or two sentences of writing guidance on each component's documentation page, plus a handful of real examples. Those few lines will do more for consistency than a 40-page tone-of-voice document nobody reads.

14.5"Ready to build": what a finished design includes

When is a component design ready to hand to engineering? Many disagreements between designers and engineers come down to different answers to that question. Agree on one checklist, and use it every time.

The design is ready when it has…

  • An anatomy diagram with every part named
  • Every option (types, sizes) and which combinations are allowed
  • Every state, including empty, loading and error
  • The stress test: long, short, translated and phone versions
  • Named values only: every colour, size and space is a token, not a number

…and also

  • Behaviour notes: what happens on click, keyboard use and resize
  • Accessibility notes: keyboard pattern, focus, what screen readers announce
  • Writing guidance: one or two lines plus examples
  • When to use it, and when to use something else instead
  • An engineer's review of the design before building starts

That last item is the most important. Bring an engineer in while the component is being designed, not after. A ten-minute conversation ("can the menu really open upwards when there's no space below?") prevents a week of rework. The best system teams pair a designer and an engineer on every component from the first sketch.

14.6Test it in the real product

A component isn't proven until it's been used in a real product by a team that didn't design it. That's why pilots matter so much (see Chapter 05). Before calling a new component stable, put it into one or two live product screens and watch what happens.

  1. Release it as "beta"

    Label it clearly as new and still settling, so teams know it might change slightly.

  2. Use it in a pilot

    One real product team uses it in real work, with a direct line to the system team.

  3. Watch for workarounds

    If the team detaches it in Figma, overrides it in code or asks "how do I make it do X?", that's design feedback.

  4. Adjust, then promote to "stable"

    Fix what the pilot revealed, then announce it as stable and ready for everyone.

Practice The review questions we always ask

Can a new designer understand when to use this in under a minute? Does it work with only a keyboard? What happens with the longest real content we've ever seen? Which existing versions will this replace, and how will teams switch? If any answer is "not sure", it isn't ready yet.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Start from real examples and real content, not a blank canvas.
  2. Design every state and stress-test every edge before handing over.
  3. Build accessibility into the component, and every screen inherits it.
  4. Agree one "ready to build" checklist, involve engineers early, and prove components in a pilot before calling them stable.

Up next →Chapter 15: Building components in code

Chapter 15

15

Building components in code

This chapter is for engineers, but it's written so that designers, product managers and founders can follow it too. Understanding how components are built in code is the best way to understand why design systems succeed or struggle.

Read this if

You build components, work closely with people who do, or keep running into "the design and the code don't match".

What you'll leave with
  1. What engineers mean by a component's "API" and "props", in plain words.
  2. How to keep design and code in step, and avoid three versions of everything.
  3. How components are tested and shipped so teams can trust them.

In this chapter

  1. 15.1What engineers mean by a component
  2. 15.2Keeping design and code in step
  3. 15.3Settings or building blocks?
  4. 15.4No hard-coded values, ever
  5. 15.5How you know a component works
  6. 15.6Packaging and shipping components

15.1What engineers mean by a component

New wordPropsThe settings you pass to a component in code, like the buttons on a TV remote: "variant", "size", "disabled".

Think of a TV remote. You don't need to know how the TV works inside. You just press buttons: volume up, channel 5, mute. A code component works the same way. Engineers use it by passing it a few settings, which they call props, and the component takes care of everything else: colours, spacing, keyboard behaviour, accessibility.

Here's what using the Ledgerly button looks like in code. Even if you've never written code, you can probably read it:

// Using the button: three settings and a label
<Button variant="primary" size="md" icon="send">
  Send invoice
</Button>

// The same button, disabled while saving
<Button variant="primary" loading>Saving…</Button>
New wordAPIThe list of settings a component accepts and what each one does. It's the "contract" between the component and the people using it.

The full list of settings a component accepts is called its API. A good component API is like a good remote: a few clearly labelled buttons that do exactly what they say, and nothing surprising. A bad one has sixty tiny buttons, half of which interfere with each other.

Once a component is in use, its API becomes a promise. If you rename variant to kind, every screen that uses the old name stops working. That's why changes to a component's API are treated as "breaking changes" (Chapter 05) and handled with care.

15.2Keeping design and code in step

In Chapter 12 we described components as twins: one in the design tool, one in code. Keeping the twins identical is one of the hardest ongoing jobs in a design system, and when it slips, things get messy fast.

ScenarioThree dropdowns, all called "Dropdown"
The situation

A mid-sized SaaS company has three engineering teams. Over two years, each built its own dropdown: one wraps an old open-source library, one is custom, and one was copied from the system and then modified.

What goes wrong

A keyboard accessibility bug is reported. It exists in all three, fixed differently in each. A design update to the dropdown takes three separate projects. New engineers don't know which one to use.

The way out

One dropdown in the system, matching the Figma version exactly; a migration guide; an automatic warning when the old ones are used; and a date after which the old ones are deleted.

One vocabulary, two places

The simplest and most effective rule: the names and options in Figma match the names and options in code, exactly. If the design file calls it "variant: primary / secondary / danger", the code does too. Not "kind", not "solid / outline", not "primary / default / destructive".

In FigmaIn codeStatus
Variant = Primaryvariant="primary"match
Size = Mediumsize="md"match (agreed short form, documented)
State = Disableddisabledmatch
Type = Tertiaryvariant="ghost"mismatch: rename one of them
Has icon = Yesicon="send"match (code also says which icon)

A shared workshop for components

Most system teams use a "workshop" tool where every component can be seen and tried in isolation, in every variant and state, outside of any product. Storybook is the most widely used one.62 It gives designers, engineers and product managers one place to look at the real coded component, which makes it much easier to spot when the twins have drifted apart. Many teams also link each Figma component directly to its code and documentation, so a designer can jump from one to the other.

Practice A monthly "twin check"

Once a month, a system designer and a system engineer spend an hour going through recently changed components side by side: Figma on one screen, the coded version on the other. List every difference and decide which twin is right. It's tedious, and it's the cheapest way we know to stop drift.

15.3Settings or building blocks?

There are two broad ways to make a component flexible, and choosing between them is one of the most important decisions in building a component library.

The first is configuration: one component with lots of settings. "Card with showImage, showAvatar, showFooter, footerAlign…" It's easy to start with, but every new need adds another setting, and eventually you get the forty-setting monster from Chapter 12.

The second is composition: several small, simple pieces that fit together, like Lego. You combine them to build exactly what you need. This is the code version of the "slots" idea from Chapter 12.

// Configuration: one component, many settings
<Card
  title="Revenue"
  showMenu
  image={chart}
  footerText="Updated 4 min ago"
  footerAlign="right"
  primaryAction="View report"
  // …and the next team will need one more
/>
// Composition: small pieces that fit together
<Card>
  <Card.Header title="Revenue">
    <Menu … />
  </Card.Header>
  <Card.Media>{chart}</Card.Media>
  <Card.Footer>
    Updated 4 min ago
    <Button>View report</Button>
  </Card.Footer>
</Card>

Neither approach is always right. Our rule of thumb is the same one we gave for design in Chapter 12. Small, frequently used components (button, checkbox, badge) should use a few clear settings, because consistency matters most and the options are limited. Bigger, container-like components (card, dialog, table, page layout) should use composition, because the content varies endlessly and settings can't keep up. Practice

15.4No hard-coded values, ever

Chapter 11 showed the button's code using only named values, with no colour codes and no pixel numbers. That's the rule for every component in the system, and it's worth enforcing automatically, because it's very easy to slip.

Imagine an engineer is fixing a small layout issue at the end of a long day. The quickest fix is to type margin-top: 13px. It works, it ships, and nobody notices. But that one value doesn't change in compact mode, doesn't follow the spacing scale, and will be wrong after the next spacing update. Multiply that by a hundred small fixes and the system's foundations are quietly bypassed.

New wordLinterA tool that automatically checks code for problems and breaks of agreed rules, and flags them before the code is merged.

The fix is a linter rule: an automatic check that flags any raw colour code, pixel value or font size in component code, and suggests the named value to use instead. It runs every time someone submits code, so nobody has to remember. The same check can run in product teams' code too, which is one of the best ways to measure how much of the product really uses the system (Chapter 03).

15.5How you know a component works

When a component is used in 400 places, a bug isn't one bug: it's 400 bugs. That's why system components are tested more thoroughly than ordinary product code. Teams usually combine four kinds of testing:

Kind of testWhat it catchesHow it works, simply
Visual testsUnintended changes to how a component looksA tool takes a picture of every variant and state and compares it with the last approved picture. Any difference is flagged for a human to check.
Automated accessibility checksMissing labels, low contrast, incorrect rolesA tool scans each component for common accessibility rule breaks. It catches a lot, but not everything.
Behaviour testsThings that don't work, like a menu that won't open with the keyboardCode that pretends to be a user: clicks, types, presses keys, and checks the right thing happens.
Manual checksWhat automation can't judgeA person tries the component with a keyboard only and with a screen reader, especially for complex components.

Visual tests deserve special mention, because they catch exactly the kind of problem from the scenario in Chapter 05, where a small padding change broke layouts. If the system team had seen pictures of every button changing size, they'd have known it was a breaking change before shipping it.

A mistake we see often

"The automated checks passed, so it's accessible"

Automated accessibility tools are excellent at catching certain problems, like missing labels and poor contrast. They can't tell whether a keyboard user can actually complete a task, or whether a screen reader announcement makes sense. Always pair them with a real keyboard and screen-reader check for interactive components.

15.6Packaging and shipping components

Finished components are bundled into a package, which is how they reach product teams. Product teams install the package, a bit like installing an app, and can update it when a new version comes out. Chapter 05 covered version numbers and breaking changes; here's what that means day to day for the people building components.

  1. Every change gets a note

    Each change includes a one-line entry for the release notes, written for the people using the system: what changed and what, if anything, they need to do.

  2. Releases happen on a rhythm

    For example, new features every two weeks and urgent fixes whenever needed. Predictable releases let product teams plan their updates.

  3. Breaking changes are rare, grouped and announced

    Collect them into one bigger release, a few times a year, with a migration guide and, where possible, a script that makes the changes automatically.

  4. Old versions get a notice period

    Product teams can't always update immediately. Say how long old versions will receive important fixes, and stick to it.

What if teams use different technologies?

Large companies often have products built with different frameworks: one team on React, another on Angular, the mobile apps in Swift and Kotlin. Named values (tokens) work everywhere, because they're generated for each platform. Components are harder, because each technology needs its own version. This is one of the biggest cost drivers in Chapter 04, and a strong reason to agree on as few front-end technologies as possible.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. A component's settings (its API) are a promise. Keep them few, clear and stable.
  2. Use exactly the same names and options in Figma and in code, and check them regularly.
  3. Small components use a few settings; big ones are built from composable pieces.
  4. Ban hard-coded values with automatic checks, test visually and for accessibility, and ship on a predictable rhythm.

Chapter 16

16

A library people can actually use

A component that nobody can find, understand or trust might as well not exist. This chapter is about the everyday side of a growing library: organising it, documenting it, tracking it, and handling the moment a team needs something a little different.

Read this if

Your Figma library has grown messy, people keep building their own versions of things that already exist, or you're not sure which components are really being used.

What you'll leave with
  1. A way to organise and name a design library so people can find things fast.
  2. A documentation template and a simple life cycle for every component.
  3. Practical ways to track usage and to handle teams that need something different.

In this chapter

  1. 16.1If people can't find it, they'll rebuild it
  2. 16.2Organising the design library
  3. 16.3Documentation that actually gets read
  4. 16.4A component's life, from idea to retirement
  5. 16.5Knowing what's actually being used
  6. 16.6When a team needs something different

16.1If people can't find it, they'll rebuild it

Here's a pattern we see in almost every growing design system. In year one, the Figma library is small and everyone knows what's in it. By year three, it has hundreds of components, several abandoned experiments, old versions nobody deleted, and names that made sense to whoever created them.

ScenarioThe designer who couldn't find the right component
The situation

Meera joins as a product designer. She needs a simple tag to show an invoice's status. She opens the library and searches "tag".

What she finds

"Tag", "Tag v2", "Chip", "Pill/Status", "Badge (old)", "Label - DO NOT USE", and three more in a page called "WIP". No descriptions. Two look identical.

What happens next

She picks one at random. It turns out to be deprecated. Engineering builds it from scratch because the code version was deleted months ago. The product now has another status tag.

Nothing in that story is about the quality of the components themselves. They may all have been well designed. The problem is findability, and in our experience it's one of the most underrated causes of low adoption. Every minute someone spends confused in your library makes building their own version more tempting.

16.2Organising the design library

A well-organised library feels like a well-organised supermarket: you can guess which aisle something is in, things are labelled clearly, and nothing out of date is left on the shelves. Here's a structure that works for most teams.

Names and descriptions

Remember Rule #3: name things so people can guess them. Use the same component names everywhere (Figma, code, documentation) and avoid version numbers or status in names. "Tag v2 NEW" is a cry for help, not a name. Status belongs in a label or description, not the name.

Most design tools let you add a short description and search keywords to each component. Use them. A good description answers "what is this for?" in one sentence and lists the words someone might search for. "Tag: a short label showing a status or category. Also known as: chip, pill, badge, label." That one line would have saved Meera half a day.

Practice Publish on a rhythm, not on a whim

Publish library updates on the same rhythm as code releases, with the same release notes. When designers get a library update notification, they should know exactly what changed and why. Random, unannounced updates teach people to ignore update notifications, and then they end up working with outdated components.

16.3Documentation that actually gets read

Layer One's ninth rule says it bluntly: docs decide adoption. People use what they can understand in the five minutes before a deadline. If documentation is long, scattered or out of date, people stop reading it and start guessing, or building their own.

The trick isn't writing more. It's writing the same few things for every component, in the same order, so people know exactly where to look. Here's the template we use:

#SectionWhat it answersKeep it to
1SummaryWhat is it, and when should I use it?One or two sentences
2When not to use itWhat should I use instead, and when?Two or three bullet points
3Live examplesWhat does it look like in each option and state?Interactive examples
4AnatomyWhat are the parts called?One labelled diagram
5How to build with itHow do I use it in code and in Figma?Copyable code, settings table, library link
6AccessibilityHow does it work with a keyboard and a screen reader? What must I add?A short checklist
7WritingWhat should the words say?One or two lines, plus examples
8Do's and don'tsWhat does correct and incorrect use look like?Two to four visual pairs
9Status and historyIs it stable? What changed recently?A status label and a short change log

The UK government's GOV.UK Design System is a good public example of documentation done well: every component page follows a consistent structure, explains when not to use it, and shares the research behind it.23 Notice also what's not in the template: long essays about design philosophy. Those belong on a separate page for people who want them.

16.4A component's life, from idea to retirement

Components aren't permanent. They're proposed, tried out, settled, and eventually replaced. Giving each stage a clear label tells everyone how much they can rely on a component right now.

The two stages teams most often skip are beta and deprecated, and they're the two that build the most trust. Beta lets you release something before it's perfect without breaking anyone's work when it changes. Deprecated lets you retire something without surprising anyone. Chapter 05 describes the deprecation process in more detail: mark it, give a guide and a notice period, track who's still using it, and only remove it in a major release.

16.5Knowing what's actually being used

You can't look after a library well if you don't know how it's used. Fortunately, both sides of the twins leave a trail.

In design files

Usage and detachments

Design tools can typically show how often each library component is inserted, and how often designers detach it (break the link to customise it). Detachments are gold: they show exactly where a component isn't meeting people's needs.

In code

Imports and versions

A simple script can count which system components each product imports, which version of the package each product uses, and where deprecated components are still in use.

ScenarioWhat the detach numbers revealed
The situation

Ledgerly's system team looks at its design library data for the first time. The alert component is used 900 times, and detached 310 times.

What they find

They look at a sample of the detached copies. Almost all of them added a second button: "Retry" next to "Dismiss". The component only allowed one.

What they do

They add an optional second action, release it in a minor update, and the detach rate drops sharply. No survey or meeting needed; the data told them.

Two cautions. First, remember Rule #8: measure time saved, not just usage. High usage is good, but it isn't the goal in itself. Second, use the data to learn, not to police. If a team detaches a component a lot, the first question is "what does the component fail to do for you?", not "why aren't you following the rules?"

16.6When a team needs something different

Sooner or later, a team will need a component to do something it doesn't do. The marketing team wants a bigger, bolder button for a campaign page. The analytics team needs a table that can freeze three columns. How you respond decides whether the system bends sensibly or breaks into pieces.

There are four common responses, and they're not equally healthy:

ResponseWhat happensWhen it's right
Extend the componentAdd a new option to the core component for everyone.When two or more teams need it and it fits the component's purpose.
Build a local componentThe team builds its own, from system parts, and owns it.When it's specific to one product. It can be promoted later.
Small overrideThe team adjusts one detail of a system component in its own code.Rarely, as a short-term fix, and always reported to the system team.
Copy and modifyThe team copies the system component's code and changes it.Almost never. The copy stops getting fixes and updates, and silently drifts.

The last row is how companies end up with three dropdowns (Chapter 15). It usually happens when the system team is slow to respond, or when "build a local component" isn't presented as a respectable option. Make the healthy paths quick and easy, and copying becomes rare.

The principle behind all of this

The system should make the right thing the easy thing. When teams work around it, treat that as feedback about the system, not a failure of the teams.

Library health checklist

  • Separate libraries for foundations, core and extensions
  • Groups that match how people think, plus a "Start here" page
  • Same names in Figma, code and docs; no versions in names
  • A one-line description and keywords on every component
  • Old versions archived and hidden; no work-in-progress published
  • One documentation template, used for every component
  • A visible life-cycle label on every component
  • Library updates published with release notes, on a rhythm
  • Usage and detach data reviewed monthly
  • Quick, respectable paths for local components

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Findability is adoption. A tidy, well-named library prevents duplicates before they happen.
  2. Document every component the same way, briefly, and say when not to use it.
  3. Label every component's stage (beta, stable, deprecated) so people know what to rely on.
  4. Use design and code data to learn where components fall short, and make the healthy paths quick and easy.

Chapter 17

17

Component complexity

A badge and a data table are both "components", but one takes an afternoon and the other can take a quarter. Understanding complexity helps you plan honestly, choose the right process for each component, and pick the simplest component that does the job.

Read this if

You estimate or plan component work, keep being surprised by how long some components take, or need to decide which component to use for a design problem.

What you'll leave with
  1. Four clear levels of component complexity, with examples.
  2. A scoring method you can use to rate any component.
  3. How complexity should change your process, and how to keep it under control.

In this chapter

  1. 17.1Not all components are equal
  2. 17.2Four levels of complexity
  3. 17.3Measuring complexity: a simple scoring method
  4. 17.4How complexity changes the way you work
  5. 17.5Choosing the simplest component that works
  6. 17.6Keeping complexity under control

17.1Not all components are equal

Here's a planning conversation we hear all the time. "This quarter, the design system team will build ten components: tooltip, badge, avatar, divider, tag, button group, breadcrumbs, tabs, date picker and data table." Ten components, three months, so about a week each. It sounds reasonable. It isn't.

Scenario"Ten components this quarter"
The situation

A system team commits to ten components in a quarter. The first six (badge, avatar, divider, tag, tooltip, breadcrumbs) are done in three weeks. The team feels ahead of schedule.

What goes wrong

Tabs take two weeks to get keyboard behaviour right. The date picker takes five weeks: time zones, locales, keyboard grids, screen readers. The data table isn't started. Leadership sees "60% done" and loses trust.

What would have helped

Rating each component's complexity first. The data table alone was more work than the other nine combined. The plan should have said so, or left it for next quarter.

Counting components is like estimating a house renovation by counting rooms: the bathroom and the hallway are both "a room", but one involves plumbing, waterproofing and tiling. Complexity is what tells you which is which. The rest of this chapter gives you a shared language for it, so designers, engineers and managers can plan together and stop being surprised.

17.2Four levels of complexity

We find it useful to sort components into four levels. They loosely echo Brad Frost's idea of building from small parts to large ones,2 but they're organised by how hard something is to get right rather than how big it is.

Level 1, elements, mostly display something: a badge, an avatar, a divider, an icon. They're about visual consistency and they're quick to build. The main risk is making too many variations of them.

Level 2, controls, are the things people interact with directly: buttons, text fields, checkboxes. Each has one main job, but now every state matters (hover, focus, disabled, error), and keyboard and screen-reader support become essential.

Level 3, composites, are built from several parts that have to work together: a menu has a trigger and a list; tabs have a tab list and panels; a dialog manages focus for everything inside it. This is where accessibility gets genuinely hard, because there are established keyboard patterns people expect, documented in the W3C's ARIA Authoring Practices Guide.61

Level 4, systems, are small applications in their own right. A data table sorts, filters, paginates, selects rows, resizes columns and must stay fast with thousands of rows. A rich text editor is a famously hard engineering problem. These components often take longer than everything else in the library combined.

17.3Measuring complexity: a simple scoring method

Levels are a good first guess, but you'll want something more precise when planning. Here's a scoring method we use. Rate the component from 0 to 3 on each of eight questions, then add them up. You don't need to be exact; the point is to have the conversation, as a team, before committing to dates. Practice

Question0 — none1 — a little2 — quite a lot3 — a lot
OptionsOne version2–3 variantsVariants × sizesMany combinations
StatesStaticHover, focusFull interactive setPlus data states (loading, empty, error)
InteractionNoneClickTyping, selectionDrag, resize, multi-select
Keyboard & screen readerNothing specialStandard tab and enterArrow keys, announcementsComplex focus management, live updates
DataNoneSimple valueLists, formattingLarge data sets, async loading
Screen sizesSame everywhereMinor adjustmentsDifferent layout on mobileDifferent behaviour on mobile
CompositionSingle partFixed sub-partsSlots or childrenNested components, coordination
PlatformsWeb onlyWeb, one frameworkWeb + one nativeWeb + iOS + Android

Then use the total like this: 0–6 is level 1, 7–12 is level 2, 13–18 is level 3, and 19–24 is level 4. Here's how three familiar components score:

ComponentOptionsStatesInteractionKeyboardDataScreensCompositionPlatformsTotalLevel
Badge1000000121 · Element
Button2211011192 · Control
Date picker23232221173 · Composite
Data table33333331224 · System

Notice the date picker. Most people would guess it's similar to a select menu. The scoring shows why it isn't: dates are data (time zones, locales, ranges, disabled days), and a calendar grid has some of the most demanding keyboard behaviour of any common component.

17.4How complexity changes the way you work

Here's the practical payoff. Once you know a component's level, you can match the process to it. Running a level 4 process for a badge wastes everyone's time; running a level 1 process for a data table guarantees bugs in production.

Level 1 · ElementsLevel 2 · ControlsLevel 3 · CompositesLevel 4 · Systems
Who's involvedOne designer, one engineerPair, plus a quick accessibility checkPair, accessibility specialist, a pilot teamA small squad, several pilot teams, product managers
ResearchInventory onlyInventory and real contentUsage research across teamsRequirements gathering, like a product feature
AccessibilityContrast, labelsKeyboard and screen-reader basicsFull ARIA pattern; manual testingExpert review; testing with assistive-technology users
TestingVisual testsVisual and behaviour testsPlus manual keyboard and screen-reader testsPlus performance tests with real data volumes
Beta periodNone neededA week or twoA month, with a pilotA quarter, with several pilots
DocumentationShort pageFull templateFull template plus behaviour notesGuides, recipes and examples
Typical effortDays1–2 weeks3–6 weeks1–3 months or more

Effort ranges are Practice estimates for one web framework, assuming foundations already exist. Each extra platform adds roughly the same again.

Practice Plan by points, not by count

Instead of "ten components this quarter", plan with the complexity totals: "about 90 points this quarter". A badge is 2 points, a data table is 22. It sounds a little nerdy, but it instantly makes plans more honest, and it gives leadership a much better picture of progress than a count of finished components.

17.5Choosing the simplest component that works

Complexity isn't just a planning tool for system teams. It's also a design decision for product teams. Every time a designer chooses a component, they're choosing a level of complexity for their users and for the engineers who'll build the screen. The simplest component that does the job is almost always the right choice.

If you need people to…Prefer this (simpler)Over this (more complex)Unless…
Choose one of 2–5 optionsRadio buttonsA dropdown selectSpace is very tight
Choose one of 6–15 optionsA selectA searchable comboboxOptions are unfamiliar or long
Choose from hundreds of optionsA combobox with searchA custom picker dialogOptions need images or grouping
Enter a date they know (birthday)Three simple fields or one text fieldA calendar date pickerThey need to see days of the week
Show extra informationText on the pageA tooltipIt's genuinely secondary
Confirm a decisionAn inline message or undoA confirmation dialogThe action is destructive and can't be undone

The date example is worth a moment. Calendar pickers feel modern, but for a date someone already knows, like their date of birth, typing it is usually faster than scrolling back decades in a calendar. The GOV.UK Design System, which is heavily user-tested, recommends simple separate day, month and year fields for exactly this case.63 Documented Simpler for the user, and a level 2 component instead of a level 3.

When you do need something complex, build it from simpler parts. A combobox is a text field plus a list plus some coordination; a data table is cells, checkboxes, buttons and menus arranged in a grid. If the simple parts are solid, the complex component inherits their quality, and fixes to the parts improve everything built from them.

17.6Keeping complexity under control

Components tend to get more complex over time. Every reasonable request adds a little: one more option, one more state, one more special case. We call this complexity creep, and it's how a level 2 button quietly becomes a level 3 problem nobody wants to touch.

Three habits keep it in check. The first is a scope statement on every component's documentation page: a short list of what this component will never do. "The button will never contain a dropdown. Use the split button instead." It sounds negative, but it saves enormous amounts of debate.

The second is splitting instead of stretching. When a component starts serving two quite different jobs, it's usually better to split it into two simpler components than to add options until it does both badly. A "card" that is sometimes a link, sometimes a form and sometimes a dashboard widget is probably three components.

The third is re-scoring once a year. Run the eight questions again for your most-used components. If a score has jumped, ask why, and whether all that complexity is still earning its keep.

A mistake we see often

Building the "universal" component

A team tries to build one table that handles every possible case: simple lists, editable spreadsheets, trees, pivot tables. It takes a year and is so complex that most teams avoid it. It's usually better to build a simple table that handles 80% of cases well, and let the rare, complex cases use a specialised component or a well-chosen third-party library.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Components range from simple elements to whole systems. A data table can be more work than ten badges.
  2. Score components on eight questions to plan honestly, and plan by points, not by count.
  3. Match the process (people, testing, beta period) to the level of complexity.
  4. Choose the simplest component that works, and fight complexity creep with scope statements and splits.

Chapter 18

18

Component architecture

Architecture sounds intimidating, but the idea is simple: decide which parts of your library are built from which, and keep those relationships tidy. Get it right and the library is easy to change for years. Get it wrong and every small change breaks something unexpected.

Read this if

You're setting up a component library, your library has become hard to change, or you want to understand how mature systems are organised under the surface.

What you'll leave with
  1. A layered model for organising components, and the rules that keep it healthy.
  2. The main ways components are put together, explained with simple examples.
  3. How to organise the files and packages, and how to manage dependencies as the library grows.

In this chapter

  1. 18.1What "architecture" means for components
  2. 18.2Layers, and the one rule that keeps them healthy
  3. 18.3Separating how it works from how it looks
  4. 18.4Four ways to put components together
  5. 18.5Organising the files and packages
  6. 18.6Dependencies, ownership and change

18.1What "architecture" means for components

Think about the wiring in a building. You don't see it, but it decides a lot: whether you can add a new socket easily, whether a fault in the kitchen trips the whole house, whether an electrician can understand it ten years later. Good wiring is organised in circuits, each with a clear job, all running back to one board.

Component architecture is the wiring of your design system. It answers three questions. What is each component built from? (A dialog uses buttons, which use text styles, which use tokens.) Which way do dependencies run? (A button can use an icon, but an icon should never need a button.) And where does each kind of logic live? (Is keyboard behaviour inside the dialog, or in a shared piece that menus use too?)

ScenarioThe text change that broke forty components
The situation

An engineer adjusts the line spacing of the library's internal Text component to fix a problem in one tooltip.

What goes wrong

Forty other components use the same Text component. Buttons grow by 2 pixels, table rows shift, and three product teams report layout bugs after the next update.

What architecture changes

A clear map of which components depend on which would have shown the "blast radius" before the change. The fix belonged in the tooltip, not in a shared building block.

18.2Layers, and the one rule that keeps them healthy

Most well-run component libraries are organised in layers, a little like the layers of a design system in Chapter 01, but zoomed in on the components themselves. Each layer is built only from the layers beneath it.

New wordPrimitiveA low-level building block, often invisible, that other components are made from: a box with spacing, a piece of styled text, a stack that spaces its children evenly.

The layer most people haven't heard of is primitives. These are tiny, mostly invisible building blocks: a Box that applies spacing and colour tokens, a Stack that lines things up with even gaps, a Text that applies a text style. Primitives mean that base components don't each reinvent "how do I apply spacing tokens". They're also handy for product teams building local components, because using primitives keeps local work on-system.

The one rule that keeps layers healthy is: dependencies only point down. A dialog may use a button. A button must never use a dialog. A primitive must never know that tables exist. When this rule is broken, you get circular dependencies (two components each needing the other), and changes start causing surprises far away from where they were made.

18.3Separating how it works from how it looks

Every interactive component has two quite different jobs. One is behaviour: what happens when you click, which element has keyboard focus, what a screen reader announces, when a menu opens and closes. The other is appearance: colours, spacing, corner rounding, text styles. Mature libraries increasingly keep these two jobs apart.

This is why headless libraries (Chapter 13) have become so popular. They provide the behaviour layer, which is the genuinely difficult part, already tested against the expected keyboard and screen-reader patterns.61 Your team supplies the appearance layer using your own tokens. The result looks entirely like your brand but behaves like a well-tested standard component.

Even if you build everything yourself, the separation is worth keeping. Put behaviour into shared pieces of logic that several components can use. A "dismiss on Escape and return focus" behaviour, for example, is needed by dialogs, side panels, menus and popovers. Write it once, test it once, and use it in all four.

18.4Four ways to put components together

When you look inside mature component libraries, you see the same few construction techniques again and again. Here they are in plain language, with a tiny code example of each for the engineers. You don't need to read the code to follow the idea.

1. Compound components: a family that works together

Some components are really a small family of parts that only make sense together. Tabs are the classic example: a list of tabs, the tabs themselves, and a panel for each tab. Instead of one giant component with dozens of settings, you provide each part separately and let them coordinate behind the scenes. It reads almost like a sentence.

<Tabs defaultValue="invoices">
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Tab value="invoices">Invoices</Tabs.Tab>
    <Tabs.Tab value="payments">Payments</Tabs.Tab>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel value="invoices">…</Tabs.Panel>
  <Tabs.Panel value="payments">…</Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>

The parts share information quietly (which tab is selected, which panel to show, where keyboard focus goes), so the person using them doesn't have to wire it up. Use this for any component made of a fixed family of parts: tabs, menus, accordions, selects.

2. Slots: spaces for any content

We met slots in Chapter 12. In code, a slot is usually just "put whatever you like here", with the component controlling the frame around it. A card with header, media, body and footer slots is the typical example. Use slots for containers whose content varies endlessly: cards, dialogs, side panels, page layouts.

3. Changing what something renders as

Sometimes you want something that looks like a button but is really a link to another page, because it navigates rather than performs an action. That distinction matters for accessibility: screen readers announce links and buttons differently, and people expect different keyboard behaviour. Many libraries let a component render as a different underlying element while keeping its appearance.

// Looks like a button, behaves like a link (because it navigates)
<Button as="a" href="/invoices/new" variant="primary">New invoice</Button>

Use this sparingly and document it clearly. "Actions use buttons, navigation uses links" is a rule worth keeping, even when they look alike.

4. Controlled and uncontrolled

Some components hold a piece of information that can change: whether a dialog is open, which tab is selected, what's typed in a field. The question is who keeps track of it. In an uncontrolled component, the component keeps track itself; you just give it a starting value. In a controlled component, the product screen keeps track and tells the component what to show. React's documentation explains the idea well.64

// Uncontrolled: "start on invoices, then look after yourself"
<Tabs defaultValue="invoices">…</Tabs>

// Controlled: "I'll tell you which tab is selected, and you tell me when it changes"
<Tabs value={tab} onValueChange={setTab}>…</Tabs>

Good libraries support both. Uncontrolled is simpler for everyday use. Controlled is needed when the screen must react to changes, for example to save the selected tab in the web address so people can share a link to it.

18.5Organising the files and packages

A tidy codebase is architecture you can see. When every component is organised the same way, engineers can find things instantly, reviewers know what to expect, and nothing important (tests, documentation, examples) gets forgotten. Here's a structure that works for most teams.

A few details matter more than they appear. The index file decides what's public. Anything not exported there is internal and can change freely, which gives the system team room to improve things without breaking anyone. The stories file shows every variant and state in the workshop (Chapter 15), which doubles as the source for visual tests. And the tokens file keeps a component's design decisions next to its code, which Chapter 20 explains.

18.6Dependencies, ownership and change

As a library grows, the relationships between components become as important as the components themselves. Nathan Curtis's series on releasing design systems devotes a whole article to this: how a change to one component travels up to everything that depends on it.28 Three habits make that manageable.

Keep a dependency map. Know which components use which. Many tools can generate this automatically from the code. Before changing a shared piece, look at what depends on it. In our scenario, that would have shown forty components relying on Text.

Name an owner for every component. In larger organisations, each component (or group of components) has a named owner who reviews changes to it. Code platforms let you record this in a simple file, so the right person is asked automatically whenever someone proposes a change.

Change the right layer. When fixing a problem, fix it at the lowest layer where it genuinely belongs, and no lower. If only the tooltip needs tighter lines, change the tooltip. If every component needs tighter lines, change the text token. The mistake in our scenario was fixing a local problem in a shared layer.

Practice Architecture review, quarterly

Once a quarter, look at the dependency map with fresh eyes. Are there arrows pointing upwards? Components nobody uses? Shared pieces with an enormous blast radius? An hour of review prevents the slow tangle that eventually makes teams say "we need to rebuild the design system".

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Organise the library in layers (tokens, primitives, base, composite, recipes) where dependencies only point down.
  2. Keep behaviour separate from appearance, so rebrands and accessibility fixes don't collide.
  3. Use compound components for families of parts, slots for containers, and support both controlled and uncontrolled use.
  4. Give every component the same file structure, a named owner and a place on a dependency map.

Chapter 19

19

Props, in depth

Props are the settings on a component: the knobs and switches people use to get the version they need. They look like a small detail, but they decide how easy a component is to use, how consistent the product stays, and how painful it is to change things later.

Read this if

You design or build components, review component proposals, or have ever wondered why some components are a joy to use and others are a puzzle.

What you'll leave with
  1. The different kinds of props, and how each one maps to Figma.
  2. Rules for designing props that are clear, safe and consistent.
  3. How props work under the surface, and how to change them without breaking anyone.

In this chapter

  1. 19.1Props are a promise
  2. 19.2The kinds of props
  3. 19.3Designing good props
  4. 19.4How props actually work
  5. 19.5Props in Figma, and documenting them
  6. 19.6Changing props without breaking anyone
  7. 19.7Prop patterns to avoid

19.1Props are a promise

Go back to the TV remote from Chapter 15. A good remote has a few clearly labelled buttons that do exactly what they say. Nobody has to read a manual to turn the volume up. Now imagine a remote where "volume up" only works if "mode B" is on, and pressing "mute" while "input 2" is selected changes the channel. That's what a component with badly designed props feels like.

Props matter for three reasons. They are the interface designers and engineers use every day, so clarity saves time on every screen. They decide consistency: if a prop lets anyone pick any colour, they will, and the product drifts. And they are a promise: once teams use a prop, changing or removing it breaks their screens, so mistakes in props are expensive to undo.

That's why mature system teams spend more time discussing props than almost anything else. A useful mindset is to treat each prop as something you'll have to support for years. Add one only when you're sure it earns its place.

19.2The kinds of props

Almost every prop in every component library falls into one of eight kinds. Knowing them helps you spot what a component needs, and spot props that don't belong.

KindWhat it doesExample in codeIn Figma
VariantPicks one approved version from a fixed listvariant="primary" | "secondary" | "danger"Variant property
SizePicks one approved sizesize="sm" | "md" | "lg"Variant property
SwitchTurns one thing on or offdisabled, loading, fullWidthBoolean property
ContentText or information to showlabel="Email", helperText="…"Text property
SlotLets you put other components insideicon={<SendIcon />}, childrenInstance swap or slot
StateThe current value, and its starting valuevalue, defaultValue, openUsually a variant ("state")
EventWhat to do when something happensonClick, onChange, onOpenChangeNot represented (prototype only)
AccessibilityExtra information for assistive technologyaria-label="Close dialog"Usually a note in the spec

The Figma column matters. Figma's component properties come in a few types (variant, boolean, text and instance swap) that line up neatly with most of these kinds.65 When the two sides use the same property names and values, a designer's choices in Figma translate directly into code, which is the "twins" idea from Chapter 12 working at the level of individual settings.

19.3Designing good props

Here are the rules we use when reviewing props. Each one comes from a mistake we've seen cause real pain.

Prefer one choice over many switches

The most common prop mistake is using several on/off switches for things that are really one choice. If a button has isPrimary, isDanger and isGhost, what happens when someone turns on two at once? Nobody knows. A single variant prop with a list of allowed values makes impossible combinations impossible.

// ✕ Three switches, eight combinations,
//   most of them meaningless
<Button isPrimary isDanger>
  Delete
</Button>
// ✓ One choice, three valid options
<Button variant="danger">
  Delete
</Button>

Use the same names everywhere

If buttons use variant, badges shouldn't use type and alerts shouldn't use kind. If buttons use size="sm", inputs shouldn't use size="small". Write down a short list of standard prop names (variant, size, tone, disabled, loading, label, onChange…) and use them across the whole library. People then learn the library once, not component by component.

Make the default the right answer

Whatever a prop is set to when nobody sets it should be the most common, safest choice. A button should default to the medium size and the secondary variant, so the "big orange button" is a deliberate decision, not an accident. A text field should default to having a visible label, not to hiding it.

Don't let props bypass the system

Props like color="#FF3300" or padding={13} let anyone escape the foundations, and someone always will. Props should offer choices from the system (tone="critical", size="lg"), never raw values.

Only require what's essential

A component should work with as few props as possible. A button needs a label and something to do when clicked; everything else should have a sensible default. Every required prop is something someone will forget.

19.4How props actually work

You don't need to be an engineer to understand the basic mechanics, and knowing them helps designers and engineers talk about components much more precisely.

Information flows one way

In most modern frameworks, information flows down through props, and news flows up through events. The screen tells the component what to show (via props). When something happens inside the component, like a click or a change, the component tells the screen (via an event prop such as onChange). The screen decides what to do, and if needed, sends new props back down.

This one-way flow is what makes components predictable. Given the same props, a component always looks the same. That's also what makes visual testing (Chapter 15) possible: render each combination of props, take a picture, compare.

Controlled and uncontrolled, again

Chapter 18 introduced the idea that either the screen or the component can keep track of a value. In terms of props, an uncontrolled component takes a defaultValue and looks after itself; a controlled component takes a value plus an event like onValueChange, and the screen stays in charge.64 Good libraries name these consistently across every component that has a value, so engineers only learn the pattern once.

Passing things through

Components should usually pass along standard properties they don't use themselves, such as an ID for testing or an accessibility attribute, to the underlying element. Engineers call this "spreading" props. It means the system doesn't block teams from doing ordinary, legitimate things, without having to add a special prop for every case.

19.5Props in Figma, and documenting them

For the twins to stay identical, props need to look the same in both places. Here's how Ledgerly's button lines up.

Code propTypeDefaultFigma propertyWhat it's for
variantprimary · secondary · dangersecondaryVariant: VariantThe importance of the action. One primary per screen area.
sizesm · md · lgmdVariant: SizeMatch the density of the surrounding UI.
iconicon namenoneBoolean Has icon + instance swap IconAn optional icon before the label.
loadingtrue / falsefalseBoolean: LoadingShows progress and prevents double clicks.
disabledtrue / falsefalseVariant: State = DisabledCan't be used right now. Explain why nearby.
childrentext—Text: LabelThe label. Start with a verb: "Send invoice".
onClickevent—— (prototype only)What happens when it's pressed.

Notice two small differences that are agreed and documented: Figma shows the icon as two properties (a switch and a choice of icon), while code uses one; and Figma treats "disabled" as a visual state, while code treats it as a switch. Differences like this are fine as long as they're written down. What causes trouble is differences nobody decided.

This table is also the right format for documentation. Every component's documentation page should list its props with the same five columns: name, type, default, the Figma equivalent and a plain-language purpose. Many teams generate the first three columns automatically from the code, so they're never out of date, and write the last two by hand.

19.6Changing props without breaking anyone

Props are promises, so changing them needs care. Here's how each kind of change should be handled, using the version-number rules from Chapter 05.

ChangeRelease typeHow to do it safely
Add a new optional propMinorGive it a default that keeps today's behaviour. Nobody notices unless they want it.
Add a new value to a variantMinorAs above. Update Figma at the same time.
Change a default valueMajorEveryone relying on the old default sees a change. Announce it, with screenshots.
Rename a propMajor (eventually)Accept both names for a while, warn when the old one is used, provide an automatic fix, remove the old name in the next major release.
Remove a prop or valueMajorDeprecate first, track usage, give a notice period, then remove.
ScenarioRenaming "kind" to "variant" across 600 buttons
The situation

Ledgerly's early button used kind. Every other component uses variant. The inconsistency confuses new engineers.

What they do

Version 4.3 accepts both kind and variant, and shows a gentle warning in development when kind is used. They publish a small script that rewrites kind= to variant= automatically.

The result

Most teams run the script in a few minutes. Usage tracking shows when the old name is gone. Version 5.0 removes kind, and nobody's screen breaks.

New wordCodemodA small script that automatically rewrites code, for example renaming a prop everywhere it's used. It turns a day of manual edits into a minute.

19.7Prop patterns to avoid

Finally, here are the prop patterns we most often recommend removing in audits. If you spot these in your library, they're usually signs of a component that's trying to do too much.

Avoid

Raw style props

color, margin, fontSize as free values. They bypass the foundations. Offer named choices instead.

Avoid

Switch explosions

Many booleans that interact. Combine related ones into a single choice.

Avoid

One-team props

A prop added for one screen in one product. It becomes everyone's maintenance burden. Build it locally instead.

Avoid

"Config" objects

A single prop that takes a big bundle of settings. It hides what the component can do and makes changes hard to track.

Avoid

Contradictory props

Props that make no sense together, like loading and disabled with different meanings. Define clearly which wins.

Avoid

Hidden behaviour

A prop whose name doesn't match what it does, like compact that also hides the icon. Names should never surprise.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Props are a long-term promise. Add one only when it earns its place.
  2. Use one choice instead of many switches, the same names everywhere, and safe defaults.
  3. Props flow down and events flow up; support both controlled and uncontrolled use.
  4. Match props in Figma and code, document differences, and change props through deprecation and automatic fixes.
