Chapter 20

20

Components and tokens

Part 02 showed how tokens hold your foundation decisions. This chapter shows how components plug into them: which parts of a component become tokens, how to name them, when a component deserves its own tokens, and how to keep the connections healthy as everything changes.

Read this if

You're connecting components to tokens, planning theming or multiple brands, or your dark mode keeps breaking in specific components.

What you'll leave with
  1. A clear map from a component's parts to the tokens it uses.
  2. A naming pattern and a decision guide for component-level tokens.
  3. How tokens connect to Figma and code, and how to audit them over time.

In this chapter

  1. 20.1Where components meet tokens
  2. 20.2Which parts of a component become tokens
  3. 20.3Naming component tokens
  4. 20.4When does a component deserve its own tokens?
  5. 20.5Tokens in Figma and in code
  6. 20.6Keeping tokens and components in sync

20.1Where components meet tokens

A quick reminder of the three levels of tokens from Chapter 07. Primitive tokens are the raw paints and sizes (brand.700, space.4). Semantic tokens name a job (action.primary.bg, text.secondary). Component tokens name a specific use inside a specific component (button.primary.background). Each level points to the one below.

The question this chapter answers is: how should a component get its values? There are two sensible answers and one bad one.

Good

Component uses semantic tokens

The button's background is action.primary.bg. Simple and enough for most single-brand products.

Good

Component has its own tokens

The button's background is button.primary.background, which points to action.primary.bg. More flexible, more to maintain.

Bad

Component uses primitives or raw values

The button's background is brand.700 or #AB2800. Dark mode and theming break here first.

ScenarioDark mode works everywhere except the date picker
The situation

Ledgerly launches dark mode. Every screen looks right, except the date picker, whose selected day stays bright orange on a white square.

The cause

The date picker was built quickly and used brand.700 and neutral.50 directly. Those are paints, not jobs, so dark mode had no way of switching them.

The fix, and the lesson

Point the date picker at job names (action.primary.bg, bg.surface) and add an automatic check that flags any component using primitives. One component fixed, a whole class of bugs prevented.

20.2Which parts of a component become tokens

Start from the component's anatomy (Chapter 12). For each part, ask: which of its visual properties could ever need to change with a theme, a brand, a density or a platform? Those properties should come from tokens. Here's the map for Ledgerly's text field.

Two things are worth noticing. First, every property that responds to a theme, brand or density is a token. Properties that never change, like the fact that the label sits above the field, are just part of the component's design and don't need tokens. Second, this map is useful even if you decide not to create component tokens. It tells you exactly which semantic token each part should use, which is what prevents the date picker problem.

20.3Naming component tokens

Component tokens multiply quickly. Ten components with ten tokens each is already a hundred names. A consistent naming pattern is what keeps them guessable (Layer One's Rule #3). This pattern works well:

{component}.{variant}.{part}.{property}.{state}

button.primary.container.background             // default state can be left out
button.primary.container.background.hover
button.primary.label.color
input.container.border.error                // no variant needed
table.row.background.selected

Use the anatomy part names from the component's documentation, so the token name, the anatomy diagram and the Figma layer names all match. Leave out levels that don't apply rather than inventing filler like "default". And use the same property words everywhere: if one component says background, none should say bg or fill.

Practice Test your names with a newcomer

Show a new designer or engineer the anatomy diagram of a component they haven't seen, and ask them to guess the token for, say, the border of the error state. If they get it right, or nearly right, your naming works. If they can't, simplify.

20.4When does a component deserve its own tokens?

Component tokens are powerful, but they have a real cost: more names to create, document and keep in step across Figma and code. Nathan Curtis has even cautioned that the industry may be "focused too much on design tokens" at the expense of other parts of a system.25 So don't create them by default. Create them when you have a reason.

SituationComponent tokens?Why
One brand, light and dark modeusually noSemantic tokens already switch with the theme.
Several brands that differ only in colourusually noA brand level under the semantic tokens handles it (Chapter 07).
Brands that style specific components differently (rounder buttons, flat cards)yesEach brand can override just those components' tokens.
White-label products where customers adjust specific componentsyesGives a safe, limited list of things customers can change.
A component that genuinely differs from the semantic ruleyes, for that partRecords the exception in one visible place instead of hiding it in code.
Native apps that need platform-specific sizesyes, for sizesiOS and Android can map component sizes to their own guidelines.

A good middle path, which many teams use, is to define component tokens only for the properties that actually vary. Ledgerly might give buttons a button.container.radius token, because one brand wants pill-shaped buttons, while letting the button's colours use semantic tokens directly. That keeps the token list short and purposeful.

20.5Tokens in Figma and in code

The connection between a component and its tokens has to exist on both sides of the twins.

In Figma

Figma's variables let designers store token values and attach them to the properties of a component's layers: a fill, a stroke, padding, corner radius.66 Variables can have several modes, such as light and dark or brand A and brand B, so switching a mode restyles every component that uses them. When the variable names match the token names in code, designers and engineers are literally talking about the same thing.

In code

The token pipeline generates the same values for code, typically as CSS variables on the web. The component's styles then reference only those names. Here's how a second brand changes just the button's shape, without touching any component code:

/* tokens: component level, in the shared format */
{
  "button": {
    "container": {
      "radius": {
        "$type": "dimension",
        "$value": "{radius.control}"
      }
    },
    "primary": { "container": { "background": {
      "$type": "color",
      "$value": "{color.action.primary.bg}"
    } } }
  }
}
/* generated CSS */
:root {
  --button-container-radius: var(--radius-control);
  --button-primary-container-background:
    var(--color-action-primary-bg);
}
/* brand B overrides one component token */
[data-brand="b"] {
  --button-container-radius: 999px;
}

/* Button.css never changes */
.button { border-radius: var(--button-container-radius); }

That's the whole point of component tokens in one picture: brand B gets pill-shaped buttons by changing one value, and no component code is touched. The token format used here is the shared Design Tokens Community Group format from Chapter 06.32

20.6Keeping tokens and components in sync

Tokens and components drift apart over time, just like Figma and code do. A component gets a quick fix with a raw value. A token is renamed but one component still uses the old name. A token is created for a feature that was later removed. A light quarterly audit catches most of this.

CheckWhat it findsHow
Raw values in componentsColours, sizes or spacing typed directly into component stylesAn automatic lint rule on every code change
Primitives used in componentsComponents pointing at paints instead of jobs (the date picker problem)A lint rule that only allows semantic and component tokens
Unused tokensTokens no component or product uses any moreA script comparing the token list with usage in code
Missing tokensProperties that change with themes but have no tokenSwitch every theme and density in the workshop and look for parts that don't change
Figma–code mismatchVariables in Figma that don't match tokens in codeCompare the exported variable list with the token source

Before changing any token, check its blast radius: which components and products use it? The same dependency map from Chapter 18 works here. A token used by one component is safe to change; a token used by forty is a release with notes and screenshots.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Components should use semantic or component tokens, never primitives or raw values.
  2. Map each part of a component's anatomy to the token it uses; that map prevents theme bugs.
  3. Create component tokens only where something genuinely varies by brand, platform or customer.
  4. Connect tokens in Figma (variables) and code (CSS variables) with matching names, and audit them every quarter.

Chapter 21

21

Components as code

Chapter 15 introduced how components are built and shipped. This chapter goes deeper: what a well-built component looks like line by line, how to style it, how to make it accessible in code, which technology to choose, and how design and engineering stay aligned once the code exists.

Read this if

You're an engineer building system components, a design lead who wants to review them with confidence, or a decision-maker choosing technologies for the system.

What you'll leave with
  1. A complete, annotated example of a well-built component.
  2. A comparison of styling approaches and technology choices.
  3. A shared definition of done and a review checklist for design and engineering.

In this chapter

  1. 21.1A well-built component, line by line
  2. 21.2Ways to style components
  3. 21.3Accessibility, in code
  4. 21.4Choosing the technology
  5. 21.5Keeping design and engineering aligned
  6. 21.6Quality beneath the surface

21.1A well-built component, line by line

Here's Ledgerly's button in React with TypeScript, two of the most common technologies for web design systems. If you don't write code, read the grey comments; they explain what each part is doing and why it matters. Everything in this chapter applies, with different syntax, to other frameworks.

// 1. The props, written down as a contract. TypeScript checks every use of the
//    button against this list, so a typo like variant="primery" is caught instantly.
type ButtonProps = {
  variant?: "primary" | "secondary" | "danger";   // one choice, not three switches
  size?: "sm" | "md" | "lg";
  icon?: IconName;                                  // a named icon from the system, not any image
  loading?: boolean;
} & React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>; // plus every normal button attribute

// 2. forwardRef lets screens reach the real button element, for focus management.
export const Button = React.forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>(function Button(
  // 3. safe defaults: secondary, medium, not loading
  { variant = "secondary", size = "md", icon, loading = false, disabled, children, ...rest },
  ref
) {
  return (
    <button                                    // 4. a real <button>: keyboard support is free
      ref={ref}
      type="button"                              // 5. never submits a form by accident
      className="button"
      data-variant={variant}                     // 6. styles read these; no colours in this file
      data-size={size}
      disabled={disabled || loading}             // 7. no double clicks while saving
      aria-busy={loading || undefined}           // 8. screen readers hear that it's working
      {...rest}                                  // 9. pass through ids, tests, aria-labels…
    >
      {loading ? <Spinner size="sm" /> : icon && <Icon name={icon} aria-hidden />}
      <span className="button__label">{children}</span>
    </button>
  );
});

A few of these lines deserve a little more explanation, because they're exactly the details that separate a system component from one built quickly for a single screen.

Using a real <button> element (comment 4) is the single most important accessibility decision in the file. Native buttons can be reached with the Tab key, pressed with Enter and Space, and are announced as "button" by screen readers, all without any extra code. Teams that build buttons out of plain boxes have to recreate all of that by hand, and usually miss something.

No colours or sizes in the file (comment 6). The component only says which variant and size it is; the stylesheet decides what that looks like, using tokens. That's why a rebrand never needs to touch this file.

Passing through everything else (comment 9) means teams can add a test ID or an accessible label without asking the system team for a new prop. The system stays small, and teams aren't blocked.

21.2Ways to style components

There are several ways to attach styles to components in code, and teams debate them passionately. The good news is that if your tokens are CSS variables, every approach can use them, so the choice matters less than it seems.

ApproachHow it works, simplyGood forWatch out for
Plain CSS with CSS variablesA normal stylesheet per component, using token variablesSimple, fast, works with any frameworkNeeds naming discipline to avoid clashes
CSS modulesLike plain CSS, but class names are made unique automaticallyNo clashes between components; easy to readRequires a build step
CSS-in-JSStyles written in JavaScript next to the componentStyles that depend on props; everything in one fileCan affect performance and server rendering; less popular than a few years ago
Utility classesMany tiny ready-made classes combined in the markupVery fast for product teams; tokens map to classesMarkup gets long; harder to enforce component-level rules

Practice Our usual recommendation

For the system's own components: plain CSS or CSS modules, reading token variables, with variants selected by data attributes as in 21.1. It's fast, framework-independent and easy for anyone to read. Product teams can then use whatever approach they like for their own screens, as long as it reads the same token variables.

Whichever approach you choose, two rules hold. Styles only ever use tokens (Chapter 20). And styles should use logical properties, such as padding-inline rather than padding-left and padding-right, so layouts mirror correctly for right-to-left languages like Arabic and Hebrew without extra work.67

21.3Accessibility, in code

Chapter 14 covered accessibility from the design side. In code, it comes down to a few habits that, once learned, become second nature.

Use the right element first

HTML already includes accessible elements for most jobs: buttons, links, form fields, labels, lists, headings, tables. They come with keyboard support and screen-reader meaning built in. Reach for extra accessibility attributes (ARIA) only when no native element fits. A common saying among accessibility specialists is that no ARIA is better than bad ARIA, because incorrect attributes can make things worse than none at all.

Follow the established patterns for complex components

For composites like menus, tabs, comboboxes and dialogs, the W3C's ARIA Authoring Practices Guide describes exactly how each should behave: which keys do what, where focus goes, what gets announced.61 Following it means your components behave the way assistive-technology users already expect. Here's what that means for a dialog:

RequirementWhat the code must do
Announce itselfIdentify itself as a dialog and use its title as its name
Move focus inWhen it opens, move keyboard focus into the dialog (usually to the first field or the close button)
Keep focus insideTab and Shift+Tab cycle within the dialog, never into the page behind it
Close on EscapeThe Escape key closes it, unless closing would lose unsaved work
Return focusWhen it closes, focus goes back to the button that opened it
Hide the backgroundThe page behind is hidden from screen readers while the dialog is open

Six requirements, every one of which a quickly built dialog tends to miss, and all of which the system's dialog solves once for every product. That's the strongest argument for building complex components centrally.

21.4Choosing the technology

A design system's components have to be built in the same technology as the products that use them. That makes technology choice one of the biggest cost decisions in the whole system (Chapter 04).

Your situationCommon approachTrade-off
All web products use one frameworkBuild components in that frameworkSimplest and best developer experience. Tied to that framework.
Web products use several frameworksWeb Components (a browser standard) or a framework-neutral core with thin wrappersOne implementation works everywhere, but integration with each framework needs care.68
Web plus iOS and Android appsShared tokens; separate native components per platformNative feel and performance, but each component is built two or three times.
Legacy products that can't adopt new componentsShip tokens (CSS variables) and styles onlyVisual consistency without rewriting, but no shared behaviour.

Whatever you choose, notice the pattern: tokens are the part that works everywhere. Components may need to be built once per technology, but tokens are generated for every platform from one source. That's why tokens come first (Rule #4), and why they're the backbone when a company has a mix of old and new technology.

21.5Keeping design and engineering aligned

Most design–engineering friction in design systems comes from one question: when is a component actually done? If designers think "done" means the Figma file is published and engineers think it means the code is merged, nothing is ever really finished. Agree one definition, for both twins.

Definition of done (both twins)

  • Figma component and code component have the same name, props and values
  • Every variant and state exists in both, and in the workshop
  • Styles use tokens only; lint passes
  • Keyboard and screen-reader behaviour tested by a person
  • Visual, behaviour and automated accessibility tests pass
  • Documentation page complete (Chapter 16 template)
  • Release note written; Figma library and code package released together

Review questions for system pull requests

  • Does this change any prop, default or visual size? Then which version number changes?
  • Which components and products depend on what's changing?
  • Do the workshop pictures show only the intended changes?
  • Is Figma updated in the same release?
  • Is any new token or prop genuinely needed by two or more teams?
  • Has someone from design reviewed the result in the workshop?

The workshop (Chapter 15) is the meeting point. Designers review the real coded component there, in every state, rather than reviewing screenshots. Many teams also link each Figma component to its code and documentation, so it's one click from design to implementation and back. The tooling varies; the habit of reviewing the real thing together is what matters.

21.6Quality beneath the surface

System components are used everywhere, so their quality affects every product's speed and stability. A few engineering concerns deserve attention even though users never see them directly.

ConcernWhy it mattersGood practice
Package sizeEvery product downloads the components it uses; heavy components slow every product.Let products import only what they use; watch size on every release.
DependenciesEach outside library a component relies on adds size, risk and upgrade work.Keep outside dependencies few and well chosen; prefer browser features.
Server renderingMany products render pages on the server for speed; components must work there too.Test components in server-rendered pages before release.
Performance with real dataA list that's fine with 20 items may freeze with 10,000.Test level 4 components with realistic data volumes (Chapter 17).
Backwards compatibilityTeams update at different speeds.Follow the versioning rules; support the previous major version for a stated time.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Good components use native elements, safe defaults, typed props, tokens only, and pass through standard attributes.
  2. Any styling approach works if it reads token variables; use logical properties for right-to-left support.
  3. Follow the established accessibility patterns for complex components, and test with a keyboard and a screen reader.
  4. Agree one definition of done for both twins, and review the real coded component together.

Up next →Chapter 22: A casebook of real situations

Chapter 22

22

A casebook of real situations

Principles are easy to agree with and hard to apply on a Tuesday afternoon with a deadline. This chapter works through twelve situations design system teams meet again and again, showing the options, what we'd recommend and why.

Read this if

You want to see how the ideas in Parts 03 and 04 play out in practice, or you're facing one of these situations right now.

What you'll leave with
  1. Worked answers to twelve common component situations.
  2. A repeatable way of thinking: options, recommendation, reasons.
  3. A migration plan you can adapt for retiring old components.

In this chapter

  1. 22.1When teams need different things
  2. 22.2Migrations: retiring the old and bringing in the new
  3. 22.3Changes that could break things
  4. 22.4When something goes wrong
  5. 22.5Pushing the limits
  6. 22.6Saying no, and listening

22.1When teams need different things

Each case follows the same shape: the situation, the realistic options, what we'd recommend, and why. They're composites of situations we see in practice, not specific clients. Illustrative

Case 1Two teams, two very different date pickers

Payments needs a picker that shows bank holidays and blocks weekends. Reporting needs to select ranges of whole months. Both ask for "the date picker".

Options

(a) One picker with options for everything. (b) Two separate pickers. (c) A solid core picker, plus extensions built on it.

Recommendation

(c). The core picker handles single dates and ranges, with a way to mark days as unavailable. Reporting builds a month-range picker as a shared extension; payments supplies its holiday list to the core picker.

Why

Option (a) creates a level 4 monster. Option (b) duplicates the hardest part, the calendar grid and its keyboard behaviour. Option (c) shares the hard part and keeps the special cases out of the core (Chapter 05, tiers).

Case 2Marketing wants a "special" button for a campaign

The campaign team wants a large gradient button with an animated arrow for a two-week launch page.

Options

(a) Add a "campaign" variant to the core button. (b) Refuse. (c) Build it locally on the campaign page, using system primitives and tokens.

Recommendation

(c), with a quick review from the system designer for accessibility (contrast on the gradient, reduced-motion support).

Why

It's a one-off with a short life. Adding it to the core makes it everyone's maintenance forever; refusing makes the system look obstructive. A local build keeps both the campaign and the core healthy.

22.2Migrations: retiring the old and bringing in the new

Case 3Three dropdowns, one system: a migration plan

The three dropdowns from Chapter 15 are used about 450 times across four products. The system now has one good dropdown. How do you move everyone across without stopping product work?

Options

(a) A "migration sprint" where every team stops and switches. (b) Leave it and hope. (c) A phased plan with tooling and a clear end date.

Recommendation

(c). See the timeline below.

Why

Big-bang migrations compete with product deadlines and usually stall halfway. Phased migrations with automation and visible progress finish.

Case 4An acquired product built with a different technology

The company acquires a startup whose product uses a different front-end framework. Leadership wants it to "look like us" within six months.

Options

(a) Rewrite the acquired product in your framework. (b) Rebuild all system components in their framework. (c) Start with tokens, then the most visible components.

Recommendation

(c). Ship your tokens as CSS variables into their product first: colours, type and spacing change in weeks. Then restyle their existing buttons, inputs and navigation to use those tokens.

Why

Tokens work in any technology (Chapter 21). They deliver most of the visual consistency for a fraction of the cost, and buy time for a proper decision about the code later.

22.3Changes that could break things

Case 5Making every button 4 pixels taller

Research shows buttons are slightly too small on touch laptops. The fix is to increase the default height from 36 to 40 pixels.

Options

(a) Ship it as a patch; it's "just a visual tweak". (b) Add a new size and leave the default alone. (c) Treat it as a breaking change, with notice.

Recommendation

(c). Release it in the next major version, with before-and-after screenshots from the workshop, a test period in a pre-release, and a note telling teams which layouts to check (table rows, toolbars).

Why

Visual changes that affect layout can break products as surely as code changes.26 Option (b) avoids the problem today but leaves most of the product with the worse default.

Case 6Renaming a widely used token

The token color.text.muted is confusingly close to color.text.subtle. The team decides to merge them into color.text.secondary.

Options

(a) Rename and fix everything at once. (b) Keep both names forever. (c) Add the new name, point the old names at it, deprecate, then remove.

Recommendation

(c). The old names become aliases of the new one, so nothing changes visually. A lint rule suggests the new name; a codemod replaces it automatically.

Why

Aliases make renaming safe. The same deprecation path used for components (Chapter 16) works for tokens.

22.4When something goes wrong

Case 7An accessibility bug found in production

A customer reports that screen readers don't announce errors in the system's text field. It's used in every form, in every product.

What to do

Confirm it, fix it in the component, add a test that would have caught it, and ship a patch release the same week. Announce it in the system channel and release notes.

Then

Check which products are on old versions that won't get the fix, and help them update. If the issue affects a legal commitment, tell the relevant owners directly.

Why it's good news

This is the system working. One fix reaches every form. Without a system, it would be dozens of separate bugs in dozens of backlogs.

Case 8A component that ignores dark mode

After launching dark mode, three components stay bright. Investigation finds raw colours and primitive tokens in their styles.

Immediate fix

Map each part of the three components to the right semantic tokens (the anatomy map from Chapter 20) and release a patch.

Prevent it

Add lint rules that block raw colours and primitive tokens in component styles. Add dark mode to every visual test.

Why

The bug isn't the three components; it's the missing guardrail. Fix the class of problem, not just the instances.

22.5Pushing the limits

Case 9A table that must handle 10,000 rows

The analytics team needs a table with 10,000 rows, frozen columns and inline editing. The system's table handles a few hundred rows comfortably and has no editing.

Options

(a) Extend the core table to do everything. (b) A specialised data grid as a separate component. (c) A well-chosen third-party grid, styled with system tokens.

Recommendation

(b) or (c), depending on how many teams need it. Keep the core table simple. If only analytics needs this, (c) is usually the fastest, safest route.

Why

Spreadsheet-like grids are a level 4 problem of their own (Chapter 17). Stretching the simple table to do it would make it worse for the 90% of screens that just need a list.

Case 10Launching in Arabic and German

The company expands into the Middle East and Germany. Arabic reads right to left; German labels are often much longer than English ones.

What to check

Do components use logical properties so they mirror automatically?67 Do labels wrap or truncate gracefully? Do icons that imply direction (arrows) flip?

What to add

Right-to-left and long-text versions in every component's stress test (Chapter 14) and in visual tests.

Why now

Fixing direction and text length once in each component is far cheaper than fixing them in every screen of every product.

22.6Saying no, and listening

Case 11"Can we add a prop just for our screen?"

An engineer asks for a hideLabelOnMobile prop on the text field, for one compact filter bar.

Questions to ask

Do other teams need this? Is there an existing way (a visually hidden label that screen readers still read)? Would it cause accessibility problems?

Recommendation

Usually: show the existing accessible way to hide a label visually, and explain why the label must remain for screen readers. No new prop.

Why

One-team props are how components grow forty settings (Chapter 19). A helpful "here's how" beats both a new prop and a flat no.

Case 12A designer who detaches everything

Library data shows one designer detaching most components they use. It looks like they're ignoring the system.

The tempting reaction

Ask their manager to enforce the rules.

The better reaction

Sit with them for an hour. In our experience, it often turns out they work on the product area the system serves worst, and their detachments are a list of what's missing.

Why

Workarounds are feedback (Chapter 16). The heaviest "rule-breakers" are often your best source of requirements.

The pattern behind all twelve cases

Keep the core simple and strict. Give special needs a respectable home outside it. Change things with notice, tools and visible progress. And treat every workaround as information.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Shared core plus extensions handles most "different needs" without bloating components.
  2. Migrations finish when they're phased, automated and visible, not when they're big-bang.
  3. Treat layout-affecting visual changes and renames as breaking; use aliases and notice.
  4. Fix the guardrail, not just the bug, and listen to the people working around the system.

05

Patterns, content and scale

Components are the words; patterns are the sentences. This final part covers how components combine into proven solutions, how words become part of the system, how a system stretches across brands, platforms and business units, the tools that keep it running, and a twelve-month plan that ties the whole book together.

  1. 23Patterns

Chapter 23

23

Patterns: from components to solutions

Components are the words of your interface. Patterns are the sentences: proven ways of combining components to solve a problem people meet again and again, like filling in a form, finding something in a long list, or recovering from an error.

Read this if

Your product has consistent components but still feels inconsistent, or teams keep solving the same problems (forms, tables, empty screens) in different ways.

What you'll leave with
  1. What a pattern is, and how it differs from a component.
  2. Practical guidance for the most common patterns: forms, tables, navigation and feedback.
  3. How to document and look after patterns as part of the system.

In this chapter

  1. 23.1Words and sentences
  2. 23.2Forms
  3. 23.3Tables, lists and finding things
  4. 23.4Navigation
  5. 23.5Feedback: loading, empty, error and success
  6. 23.6Documenting and looking after patterns

23.1Words and sentences

You can have a perfect dictionary and still write confusing sentences. The same thing happens with design systems. Every team uses the system's button, text field and table, so the components are consistent, but each team combines them differently. One form shows errors at the top, another under each field, a third in a pop-up. One list paginates, another scrolls forever. The product still feels like several products.

New wordPatternA proven, documented way of combining components to solve a recurring user problem, such as "how we validate a form" or "how we show that there are no results".

That's what patterns fix. A pattern isn't a new component. It's guidance on how to use existing components together to solve a specific problem, with the reasoning and research behind it. The UK government's GOV.UK Design System is the best-known public example: alongside its components, it publishes patterns for things like asking for dates, addresses and names, each based on research with real users.63 Documented

ScenarioFour ways to say "nothing here"
The situation

A Ledgerly customer searches invoices, filters payments, opens an empty report and views a new project. Every component on those screens comes from the system.

What they see

"No data", a blank white area, a sad-face illustration with "Oops!", and "0 results found" in small grey text. Four teams, four different answers to the same question.

What a pattern changes

One documented empty-state pattern with three versions (first use, no results, cleared), each with a clear message and a next step. Same components, now saying the same thing.

23.2Forms

Forms are where products make money and where users get most frustrated, so they're usually the first pattern worth writing down. Here's the guidance we start from. Practice

QuestionOur default answerWhy
LayoutOne column, labels above fieldsEasiest to scan; works on every screen size; labels stay close to their fields.
Required fieldsMark the optional ones ("optional") rather than starring the required ones, when most fields are requiredFewer marks, less noise; clear wording beats a symbol.
When to check for errorsWhen the person leaves a field (for format problems) and when they submit (for everything)Checking while someone is still typing shows errors before they've finished.
Where to show errorsA message next to each problem field, plus a summary at the top on submit that links to each errorPeople and screen readers can find every problem; the GOV.UK error summary is a well-tested model.69
What errors sayWhat's wrong and how to fix it: "Enter a date after 1 January 2026"Errors must be identified and described in text.70 Standard
Long formsSplit into steps with a clear progress indicator, or into sections with headingsSmaller chunks feel achievable and reduce mistakes.
ButtonsOne primary action at the end, labelled with what it does ("Send invoice")The main action should be obvious and specific.

The point isn't that these answers are the only right ones. Some products have good reasons to differ. The point is that your product has one answer for each question, written down, so every form feels familiar and every team stops re-debating the same choices.

23.3Tables, lists and finding things

Most business software is, at heart, a collection of lists: invoices, customers, orders, users. How people find, sort and act on items in those lists decides how fast they can work.

Table, list or cards?

Table

When people compare

Many items with the same attributes, where people scan columns, sort and compare: invoices, transactions.

List

When people pick

Items with one or two key details, where people mostly find one and open it: messages, notifications.

Cards

When items are visual

Items where an image or a preview matters more than comparison: templates, projects, products.

Pagination, "load more" or endless scrolling?

ApproachBest forDownsides
PagesWork tools where people need to find their place again or reach the endExtra clicks; page size choice matters
"Load more" buttonFeeds and search results where people mostly look at the first fewLong pages; footer hard to reach after loading lots
Endless scrollingBrowsing content with no particular goalHard to return to a spot; footer unreachable; heavy for keyboard and screen-reader users

Search, filters and bulk actions

Write down how filters work across the product: where they sit (above the list, or in a side panel), whether results update instantly or after pressing "Apply", how active filters are shown and cleared, and what the empty result looks like. For bulk actions, decide once how people select many items (checkboxes, with a "select all on this page" option), where the actions appear (a bar that appears when items are selected), and how destructive bulk actions are confirmed. These small decisions, made consistently, are what make a large product feel learnable.

23.4Navigation

Navigation is the pattern people notice least when it works and most when it doesn't. The system should define the app frame (Chapter 10) and the rules for moving around inside it.

ComponentUse it forDon't use it for
Side menuThe main sections of an app with many areas (5+)Actions; settings for the current page
Top navigationA few main sections (up to about 5), often on websitesDeep hierarchies
TabsSwitching between views of the same thing (an invoice's details, payments, history)Moving between different areas of the app
BreadcrumbsShowing where you are in a deep hierarchy and stepping back upFlat products with one or two levels
Back linkReturning from a detail page or a step in a flowReplacing the browser's own back button behaviour

Practice Three levels is usually enough

If people need to go more than three levels deep to reach something they use often (section, page, tab), the problem is usually the structure of the product, not the navigation component. That's a conversation for product leadership, and the design system is often the first to notice it.

23.5Feedback: loading, empty, error and success

Every screen has moments when things aren't normal: data is loading, there's nothing to show, something went wrong, or something just succeeded. These moments are where products most often feel inconsistent, because each team handles them as an afterthought.

Choosing how to tell people something

ComponentUse when the message is…Example
Inline messageAbout one specific field or section"Enter a full email address" under the field
ToastA short confirmation that needs no action, and that it's fine to miss"Invoice sent"
BannerAbout the whole page or account, and important enough to stay visible"Your trial ends in 3 days"
DialogSomething people must decide before they continue"Delete this customer and 12 invoices?"

Loading

For short waits, show a skeleton (grey shapes where the content will appear) so the page doesn't jump when it loads. For actions like saving, show progress on the button that was pressed. For long operations, show what's happening and, if possible, how long it will take. And always handle the case where loading fails, with a clear way to try again.

Empty states

First use

Nothing yet

Explain what will appear here and offer the first step: "No invoices yet. Create your first invoice to get paid faster."

No results

Search or filters found nothing

Say what was searched, and suggest changing or clearing filters.

All done

Everything is cleared

A small, positive confirmation: "All invoices are paid." No action needed.

23.6Documenting and looking after patterns

Patterns need documentation even more than components do, because there's no code to copy: the guidance is the pattern. A consistent template helps.

#SectionWhat it covers
1The problemWhat people are trying to do, in one or two sentences
2The solutionHow we solve it, which components are used, and in what arrangement
3ExamplesReal screens from your products, good ones and ones to improve
4VariationsApproved versions for different situations (for example, a short form vs a long one)
5When not to use itSituations where a different pattern fits better
6EvidenceResearch, test results or analytics that support the approach
7Accessibility and writingKeyboard flow, announcements, and the words to use

Patterns change more often than components, because they're closer to product decisions. Give each pattern an owner, often a senior product designer rather than the system team, and review patterns when research or analytics suggest something isn't working. When a pattern becomes stable and is built the same way everywhere, it may be worth turning into a "recipe" or composite component (Chapter 18), so teams can use it rather than rebuild it.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Patterns are documented ways of combining components to solve recurring problems.
  2. Start with forms, lists, navigation and feedback states; these cause the most inconsistency.
  3. Have one written answer to each recurring question, with reasons, and evidence where you have it.
  4. Document patterns with a consistent template, give each an owner, and promote stable ones into recipes.

Up next →Chapter 24: Content and language in the system

Chapter 24

24

Content and language in the system

A product can have perfectly consistent buttons and still feel chaotic if one says "Remove", another "Delete" and a third "Discard" for the same action. Words are part of the interface, so they belong in the design system too.

Read this if

Your product's wording feels inconsistent, you're about to translate your product, or writers and designers keep debating the same phrases.

What you'll leave with
  1. How to define a voice and adjust tone for different moments.
  2. A shared vocabulary and reusable writing formulas.
  3. What it takes to write for everyone, and to prepare for translation.

In this chapter

  1. 24.1Why words belong in the system
  2. 24.2Voice and tone
  3. 24.3A shared vocabulary
  4. 24.4Formulas for common messages
  5. 24.5Writing for everyone
  6. 24.6Getting ready for other languages

24.1Why words belong in the system

People read interfaces in fragments: a button label, a heading, an error message. When those fragments use different words for the same thing, people hesitate. Is "Archive" the same as "Remove"? Will "Discard" lose my work? Is a "workspace" the same as an "organisation"? Every hesitation is a small cost, and in a large product they add up.

ScenarioFive words for "make it go away"
The situation

Across Ledgerly, removing something uses "Delete", "Remove", "Archive", "Discard" and "Clear", chosen by whoever built each screen.

What goes wrong

Customers can't tell which actions are permanent. Support tickets ask how to recover "archived" invoices that were actually deleted. Translators get five different words to translate.

What the system adds

A vocabulary entry: "Delete = permanent, always confirmed. Archive = hidden, recoverable. Remove = taken out of a list, not deleted." Three words, three meanings, used everywhere.

Content in a design system usually covers four things: voice and tone (how the product sounds), vocabulary (which words mean what), formulas (reusable shapes for common messages) and localisation rules (what has to work in other languages). None of it needs to be long. A few pages, well maintained, do more than a 40-page style guide nobody opens.

24.2Voice and tone

Think of the difference between personality and mood. Your voice is your product's personality: it stays the same everywhere. Your tone is the mood: it adapts to the moment, the way a good colleague speaks differently when celebrating a win and when delivering bad news.

Ledgerly's voice, for example, might be: clear, calm and helpful. Its tone then adjusts:

MomentToneExample
SuccessBrief and warm. Don't over-celebrate routine tasks."Invoice sent to Acme Ltd."
ErrorCalm and specific. Never blame the person."We couldn't process this payment. The bank declined it. Try another card."
WarningClear about the consequence, and what to do."This invoice is overdue by 14 days. Send a reminder?"
Destructive actionSerious and explicit. Name exactly what will happen."Delete this customer? Their 12 invoices will also be deleted. This can't be undone."
First useEncouraging and practical. Point to the next step."No invoices yet. Create your first one to get paid faster."

A mistake we see often

Jokes in error messages

"Oops! Something went wonky!" might feel friendly in a design review. To someone whose payroll just failed, it feels dismissive. Keep personality for calm moments; in stressful moments, be clear and kind.

24.3A shared vocabulary

The single most useful content artefact is a simple vocabulary list: the words your product uses, what they mean, and the words to avoid. It helps designers, engineers, support and translators all at once.

UseMeaningDon't use
DeletePermanently remove. Always confirmed.Destroy, erase, discard
ArchiveHide from the main list; can be restored.Hide, store
CustomerA business you invoice.Client, account, buyer
WorkspaceYour company's area in Ledgerly, shared by its team.Organisation, tenant, account
Sign in / Sign outStart or end a session.Log in, login, log out
Due dateThe date an invoice must be paid by.Deadline, payment date

Small rules that add up

A handful of formatting rules prevent a surprising amount of inconsistency. Decide them once: sentence case or title case for headings and buttons (we recommend sentence case: "Send invoice", not "Send Invoice"); how dates are written; whether numbers use words or digits; how currencies are shown; and whether you write "you" and "your" when addressing people (we recommend it). Put them on one page, next to the vocabulary.

24.4Formulas for common messages

Most interface text falls into a few types of message. Giving each type a simple formula means anyone can write a good message, quickly, in the product's voice. Chapter 14 introduced the idea for individual components; here are the formulas side by side.

MessageFormulaExample
ButtonVerb + object"Send invoice", "Add customer"
ErrorWhat happened + why (if known) + what to do"Payment failed. The card has expired. Update the card details."
Field errorWhat to enter, specifically"Enter an amount between ₹1 and ₹10,00,000"
Confirmation dialogQuestion naming the action + consequence; buttons repeat the action"Delete 3 invoices? This can't be undone." [Delete invoices] [Cancel]
Empty stateWhat will appear here + how to start"Your payments will appear here. Connect a bank account to get started."
SuccessWhat happened, briefly"Customer added."

Notice the confirmation dialog's buttons. "Delete invoices" and "Cancel" are far clearer than "Yes" and "No", because people often read only the button. This one small habit prevents a lot of accidental deletions.

24.5Writing for everyone

Good interface writing is accessible writing. Plain words, short sentences and clear structure help everyone, and they matter most for people reading in a second language, people with cognitive or learning disabilities, and anyone who is tired, stressed or in a hurry.

PrincipleIn practice
Plain words"Use" not "utilise"; "start" not "initiate"; explain jargon or avoid it.
Front-load meaningPut the important words first: "Invoice sent", not "We have successfully sent your invoice".
Descriptive links"View payment history", not "Click here". Screen-reader users often navigate by a list of links.
Meaningful image textDescribe what an image tells people; mark purely decorative images so screen readers skip them.
Inclusive languageAvoid assumptions about gender, ability or culture; use "they" when you don't know; avoid idioms that don't translate.
Don't rely on direction or colour"Select the highlighted option" or "click the button on the right" fails for many people. Name the thing.

24.6Getting ready for other languages

Even if you only support one language today, a few habits now will save a painful rebuild later. Translation touches components, patterns and code, so it's very much a design system concern.

HabitWhy it matters
Leave room for longer textMany languages need noticeably more space than English for the same message. Components should wrap or grow, not cut text off.
Support right-to-leftArabic and Hebrew read right to left; layouts and directional icons should mirror. Logical CSS properties make this mostly automatic.67
Never build sentences from pieces"You have " + count + " invoices" breaks in languages with different word order or plural rules. Keep whole sentences together, with placeholders.
Handle plurals properlySome languages have several plural forms, not just "one" and "many". Use your platform's built-in plural rules.71
Format dates, numbers and money by locale"1,00,000" in India is "100,000" elsewhere; dates differ too. Use built-in formatting rather than hand-written formats.71
Give translators context"Post" could be a verb or a noun. Add a note or a screenshot to every string.

Who owns the words?

In larger companies, content designers or UX writers own the voice, vocabulary and formulas, just as system designers own the visual foundations. In smaller ones, it's often a senior designer or product manager with a little protected time. Either way, treat content guidance like any other part of the system: it has an owner, it's versioned, changes are announced, and teams can propose improvements. Some teams even add simple automatic checks, flagging words from the "don't use" list in code reviews.

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Words are part of the interface; inconsistent words confuse people as much as inconsistent buttons.
  2. Keep one voice, adjust the tone to the moment, and be calm and specific when things go wrong.
  3. A short vocabulary list and a few message formulas do more than a long style guide.
  4. Write plainly and inclusively, and build components and code ready for other languages from the start.

Up next →Chapter 25: Scaling across products, brands and platforms

Chapter 25

25

Scaling across products, brands and platforms

A design system that works beautifully for one product and one team gets tested in new ways when the company grows: a second brand, a mobile app, an acquisition, a new business unit with its own ideas. This chapter is about stretching the system without breaking it.

Read this if

Your system needs to serve several brands, several platforms or several business units, or you're planning for that future.

What you'll leave with
  1. How to support several brands and platforms from one source of decisions.
  2. How "families of systems" work, and when you need one.
  3. Governance and funding models that work across business units.

In this chapter

  1. 25.1What changes when you scale
  2. 25.2Several brands from one system
  3. 25.3Several platforms from one source
  4. 25.4Families of systems
  5. 25.5Governance and funding across business units
  6. 25.6Legacy products and long migrations

25.1What changes when you scale

Scaling a design system isn't just "the same thing, bigger". New kinds of difference appear: different brands that must look different, different platforms that must feel native, and different business units with different priorities and budgets. Each one tempts teams to start their own system.

ScenarioOne group, three brands, three systems
The situation

A financial group runs three consumer brands: a bank, an insurance company and a lending app. Each brand has its own design team, and each built its own design system.

What goes wrong

Three teams maintain three date pickers, three accessibility fixes, three token pipelines. When a regulation changes the rules for how fees must be displayed, it's implemented three times, differently.

What scaling well looks like

One shared core (behaviour, accessibility, structure, foundations) with a brand layer on top. Each brand still looks like itself; the hard work is done once.

The guiding principle for everything in this chapter is simple: share what should be the same, and make what should differ easy to differ. Behaviour, accessibility and structure should almost always be shared. Visual identity, and sometimes platform conventions, should be allowed to vary, in controlled ways.

25.2Several brands from one system

Chapter 07 introduced brand tokens, and Chapter 20 showed how component tokens let a brand restyle specific components. Put together, they make a multi-brand system practical. Here's what usually stays shared and what varies.

LayerShared across brandsVaries by brand
BehaviourKeyboard use, focus, announcements, validation logicNothing
StructureComponent anatomy, props, patternsRarely; only through agreed extensions
Semantic tokensThe names of the jobsWhich values the names point to
ColourThe lightness curve and contrast rulesBrand hues, and sometimes neutral tints
TypographyThe roles (heading, body, label) and accessibility rulesFont families, sometimes the scale
Shape and motionThe token namesCorner rounding, shadows, animation style
Imagery and voiceAccessibility rulesIllustrations, photography, tone of voice

The result is that a new brand is mostly a new set of values, not a new system. Because the lightness curve is shared (Chapter 07), every brand's colours meet the same contrast rules automatically, even when their hues are completely different. A regulation change to how fees are shown becomes one pattern update, inherited by all three brands.

Practice Test with the most different brand first

When building a multi-brand system, design the first components against your two most different brands at once, not one brand first. It's much easier to find the right flexibility points while building than to add them afterwards.

25.3Several platforms from one source

Web, iPhone and Android each have their own conventions. Apple's guidelines and Google's Material Design describe different navigation, different controls and different text sizes.7252 A good multi-platform system respects those conventions while keeping the brand and the experience recognisably the same.

Decide to…UsuallyExamples
ShareBrand, foundations, content, component names and purposesColours, voice, "primary button", error message formulas
AdaptThings where the platform has strong conventionsNavigation patterns, date pickers, switches, text sizes, haptics
Keep separateThings that only exist on one platformWidgets, watch faces, keyboard shortcuts on desktop

A useful test: would a regular user of this platform be surprised by how this behaves? If yes, adapt to the platform. If no, share it. People expect an iPhone app to feel like an iPhone app, while still recognising your brand.

25.4Families of systems

At a certain size, one system can't sensibly hold everything. A bank's customer app, its internal operations tools and its marketing site have such different needs that forcing them into one library makes it worse for all three. The answer many large companies arrive at is a family of systems: a shared core, with specialised systems built on top of it.

A family of systems only works with a few clear rules. Everyone uses the core tokens, so the brand and accessibility baseline stay consistent. Specialised systems build on core components rather than copying them, so fixes flow outwards. Each specialised system has a named owning team, usually the one closest to its users. And things move into the core when they're needed widely, following the rule of two from Chapter 05. Without these rules, a family of systems slowly becomes the "22 separate systems" problem again.

25.5Governance and funding across business units

When several business units depend on one system, two questions become political very quickly: who decides, and who pays. Answering them openly, early, prevents a lot of quiet resentment.

Who decides

Most large organisations settle on a small council: the system lead plus a design and engineering representative from each major business unit, meeting on a regular rhythm for decisions that affect everyone (foundations, breaking changes, the roadmap). Day-to-day decisions stay with the system team and contributors, as described in Chapter 05. The council is for the few decisions that genuinely need everyone in the room.

Who pays

Funding modelHow it worksWorks well whenRisk
Central budgetThe system is funded centrally, like shared infrastructureLeadership sees the system as a platformBusiness units feel no ownership
Contribution of peopleEach business unit gives a share of designers and engineers to the systemUnits are similar in size and needContributed people get pulled back to unit work
MixedA central core team plus contributors funded by units for their extensionsMost mature, multi-unit organisationsNeeds clear rules about core vs extension
Scenario"Our unit wants to opt out"
The situation

One business unit complains the system is too slow for its needs and asks to build its own.

What to do

Treat it as feedback first: what's missing, and why is it slow? Often the answer is an extension owned by that unit, built on the core, with a fast lane for their needs.

Why

Opting out fully costs the unit the shared accessibility, brand and maintenance work, and costs everyone consistency. A well-supported extension usually gives them the speed they want without either cost.

25.6Legacy products and long migrations

At scale, there's always an older product that can't adopt the new system quickly: different technology, no team assigned, or a complete rewrite planned "next year". Don't let these products hold the system back, and don't leave them behind entirely.

  1. Tokens first

    Ship the token values (as CSS variables or a theme file) into the legacy product. Colours, type and spacing align quickly, and the product looks part of the family (Chapter 22, case 4).

  2. Replace the most visible parts

    Navigation, buttons and forms, where users notice inconsistency most. Replace them as screens are touched, not all at once.

  3. Measure the whole portfolio

    Track adoption per product on one simple dashboard, so leadership sees progress across the whole company, not just in the newest products.

  4. Agree an end state

    For each legacy product, decide openly: full adoption, tokens only, or retirement. A clear plan is better than an endless "someday".

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Share behaviour, accessibility and structure; let brand and platform conventions vary in controlled ways.
  2. One token source can feed every brand and platform; components are built natively with the same names.
  3. At large scale, use a family of systems: a shared core plus specialised systems with named owners.
  4. Decide openly who decides and who pays, and bring legacy products along with tokens first.

Up next →Chapter 26: Tools, automation and AI

Chapter 26

26

Tools, automation and AI

Tools don't make a design system, but the right ones make it much cheaper to run. This chapter maps the toolchain of a typical system, shows which automation pays back first, and looks practically at where AI helps today, and where it doesn't.

Read this if

You're choosing tools for a design system, spending too much time on manual upkeep, or wondering how AI fits into design system work.

What you'll leave with
  1. A map of the tools a design system uses, and what each one is for.
  2. The minimum tool set for each stage of maturity, and the automations worth building first.
  3. Realistic, useful ways to use AI in design system work, with the cautions that matter.

In this chapter

  1. 26.1Tools serve the process, not the other way round
  2. 26.2The toolchain, mapped
  3. 26.3The right tools for your stage
  4. 26.4Automation that pays for itself
  5. 26.5Where AI helps today
  6. 26.6Using AI responsibly

26.1Tools serve the process, not the other way round

It's tempting to start a design system by choosing tools: a documentation platform, a token manager, a component workshop. Tools feel like progress. But a tool without an owner and a process quickly becomes an expensive, out-of-date mirror of what's really happening.

ScenarioThe documentation site nobody updated
The situation

A company buys a polished documentation platform and spends a month filling it with beautiful pages for every component.

What goes wrong

Nobody's job includes keeping it current. Within six months, half the pages describe old versions. Teams stop trusting it and ask in Slack instead.

What would have worked

Docs as part of the definition of done (Chapter 21), with parts generated from code automatically, so updating them is part of shipping, not a separate chore.

So the order matters: decide how the system will work (Chapter 05), then pick tools that make that way of working easier. Layer One's seventh rule applies here too: build where the system lives. Put the system into the files, repositories and tools your teams already use every day, rather than asking them to visit somewhere new.

26.2The toolchain, mapped

Most design systems use tools in six areas. You don't need something in every area on day one, but it helps to see the whole picture and how the pieces connect.

26.3The right tools for your stage

A startup doesn't need an enterprise toolchain, and an enterprise can't run on a shared spreadsheet. Here's the minimum tool set we'd suggest for each of the maturity stages from Chapter 02. Add more only when a real problem calls for it. Practice

StageDesignTokensCodeDocsQuality and insight
1 · Shared stylesOne Figma libraryA shared file of valuesThemed off-the-shelf libraryA single pageDesign reviews
2 · Basics in codeLibrary + variablesToken files + build toolYour package + workshopWorkshop pagesLint for raw values
3 · Looked afterLibraries split by purposeLight and dark modesVersioned releasesA docs siteVisual and accessibility tests; usage scripts
4 · PlatformBrand and platform librariesMulti-brand, multi-platformSeveral packages and platformsDocs platform with searchHealth dashboard; automated migrations

Practice Keep your decisions portable

Whatever tools you choose, keep your tokens in the shared, vendor-neutral format and your components in your own repository. Tools come and go; your decisions shouldn't be locked inside any single product.

26.4Automation that pays for itself

Every hour the system team spends on repetitive upkeep is an hour not spent helping product teams. These automations, roughly in the order we'd build them, give the best return. Practice

#AutomationWhat it savesEffort
1Token pipelineHand-copying values into code and design; mismatches between themDays
2Lint rulesHard-coded colours and spacing slipping in; reviewers policing by handDays
3Visual regression testsAccidental visual changes; nervousness about every release1–2 weeks
4Automated accessibility checksCommon accessibility mistakes reaching productsDays
5Release notes from changesWriting release notes from memory at the last minuteDays
6Usage dashboardGuessing which components and versions are used where1–2 weeks
7Codemods for migrationsTeams manually rewriting code for breaking changesPer change

Notice that the first two are cheap and prevent the most common problems in the whole book: values drifting between design and code, and hard-coded values bypassing the foundations. If you automate nothing else, automate those.

26.5Where AI helps today

AI tools are changing design system work quickly, and it's easy to either overhype them or dismiss them. Here's a grounded view of where they genuinely help, based on how teams are using them now. Layer One's founder has worked on exactly this kind of tooling: AI-assisted drafting of company-wide design patterns, and tools that check design files and code against a design system for hundreds of designers and over a thousand engineers.1

UseHow it helpsKeep a human…
Drafting documentationTurns a component's code, props and examples into a first draft of its documentation page…to check accuracy and add the "when not to use" judgement
Writing release notesSummarises code changes into plain-language notes for product teams…to judge what's breaking and what teams must do
Checking against the systemFlags designs or code that use off-system colours, spacing or components, and suggests the system equivalent…to decide when a deviation is deliberate and fine
Answering "which component?"An assistant that has read your docs answers everyday questions in chat…to keep the docs it reads accurate
MigrationsHelps write and apply codemods for renames and replacements…to review every change before it merges
Drafting patternsProposes a first pattern write-up from examples across products…to bring research, evidence and taste

There's a pattern in that table. AI is good at drafting and checking, and it's only as good as the information it's given. A well-structured system, with named tokens, consistent props, documented components and clear rules, turns out to be excellent input for AI tools. A messy one gives messy results. In that sense, the work in this book is also the best preparation for using AI well.

26.6Using AI responsibly

A few cautions are worth taking seriously, because the cost of a design system mistake is multiplied across every product.

Watch out for

Confident mistakes

AI tools can produce plausible but wrong documentation or code. In a system used by hundreds of people, a wrong statement in the docs spreads quickly. Review everything.

Watch out for

Accessibility by assumption

Generated components often look right but miss keyboard behaviour or announcements. Test them like any other component (Chapter 21).

Watch out for

Inventing new things

Ask an AI to "build a settings page" and it may invent components and colours instead of using yours. Point it at your system and check the result against it.

Watch out for

Confidentiality

Unreleased designs and internal code are sensitive. Use tools your company has approved, with appropriate data protections.

Questions to ask before adopting any tool

  • What problem does it solve that we actually have today?
  • Who will own it and keep it current?
  • Does it work with our existing files, repositories and formats, or does it lock our decisions in?
  • How will we know, in three months, whether it was worth it?
  • What happens to our work if we stop using it?

The short version

What to remember from this chapter

  1. Decide how the system works first; choose tools that make that easier, and keep decisions portable.
  2. Match the toolset to your maturity stage. More tools aren't better.
  3. Automate the token pipeline and lint rules first; they prevent the most common problems.
  4. Use AI for drafting and checking, keep humans for judgement, and remember that a well-structured system makes AI far more useful.

Putting it all together: your first twelve months

You've seen the whole system: why it matters, what it costs, how to run it, its foundations, its components and how it scales. This final chapter turns all of that into a practical plan for your first year, the rhythms that keep a system healthy, and one checklist for the whole journey.

Read this if

You're about to start (or restart) a design system and want a single plan that connects everything in this book.

What you'll leave with
  1. A quarter-by-quarter plan across foundations, components, operations and adoption.
  2. The weekly, monthly and quarterly rhythms of a healthy system.
  3. A master checklist, and the ten most common ways systems fail.

In this chapter

  1. 27.1The whole book on one page
  2. 27.2A twelve-month plan
  3. 27.3The rhythms of a healthy system
  4. 27.4The master checklist
  5. 27.5Ten ways design systems fail, and the antidote
  6. 27.6A closing note

27.1The whole book on one page

Before the plan, here's how the five parts of this book fit together. Each part answers a different question, and each one depends on the parts before it.

If you remember only one idea from the whole book, make it this one: a design system is an agreement, not a library. The components, tokens and documentation are how the agreement is written down. The people, processes and rhythms are how it stays alive.

27.2A twelve-month plan

Here's a realistic first year for a mid-sized product company, like Ledgerly, starting from Stage 1 or 2 (Chapter 02). It runs four workstreams side by side. Each quarter ends with a gate (Chapter 04): something you can point to that earns the next quarter's investment. Illustrative

Quarter 1 · StartQuarter 2 · ProveQuarter 3 · SpreadQuarter 4 · Settle
FoundationsAudit. Colour, type, spacing, layout as tokens. Token pipeline.Semantic tokens complete. Contrast checks automated.Dark mode as a second theme.Density modes. Token audit.
Components8 basics: button, field, select, checkbox, radio, switch, link, alert.Containers and feedback: dialog, card, tabs, toast, menu, empty state.Data and navigation: table, pagination, badge, tag, side menu.The hard ones: date picker, search, advanced table features.
OperationsOwner named. Who-decides-what agreed. Versioning rules written.Request and contribution process live. Docs template.First outside contribution. Monthly health check.Deprecation of old components. Next year's roadmap.
AdoptionPilot team: new settings page.Pilot two: onboarding. Champions in each team.Second and third teams adopt. Office hours.Migration dashboard. Most new work on the system.
GateThe pilot ships using only tokens.The pilot team is measurably faster or has fewer UI bugs.A team adopts without hand-holding.Adoption trend and savings reported to leadership.

Two things make this plan work. First, every quarter delivers something teams can use immediately, so the system earns trust as it goes. Second, the components are always built inside a real product project (a pilot), never in isolation. That's Dan Mall's advice from Chapter 05, and in our experience it's the single biggest predictor of a system that people actually use.29

27.3The rhythms of a healthy system

A design system stays healthy through steady habits, not heroic efforts. Here are the rhythms we set up with every team. Put them in the calendar in the first month; they're much harder to add later. Practice

How oftenWhatWhyChapter
DailyAnswer the support channelFast answers keep people using the system instead of working around it05
WeeklyOffice hours; triage new requestsHelp teams build with the system; decide one-off vs shared quickly05, 13
Every two weeksRelease, with notes for usersA predictable rhythm lets teams plan updates05, 15
MonthlyHealth check; Figma–code "twin check"; usage and detach dataSpot drift and problems early05, 15, 16
QuarterlyArchitecture and token audit; debt review; roadmap update; council (at scale)Prevent slow tangles; keep the plan honest18, 20, 25
YearlyRe-score component complexity; satisfaction survey; budget and staffing reviewStep back and decide the next stage04, 17

27.4The master checklist

Every chapter ended with its own checklist. Here's the condensed version for the whole journey. Use it as a quarterly review: anything unticked becomes a candidate for the next quarter's plan.

Decide and fund Part 01

  • An audit with "before" numbers
  • A sponsor, engineering commitment and a named owner
  • The next maturity stage chosen, not the last one
  • A budget in people and months, funded in steps
  • An ownership model and a who-decides-what table

Foundations Part 02

  • OKLCH palette; colours named by job; contrast tested
  • Text styles by role; 4px spacing scale; breakpoints
  • One token source feeding design and code

Components Part 03

  • Components chosen by frequency and pain
  • Every state designed; "ready to build" checklist
  • A tidy, documented library with life-cycle labels

Architecture Part 04

  • Complexity scored; process matched to level
  • Layers with downward-only dependencies
  • Consistent props, matched in Figma and code
  • Components use semantic or component tokens only
  • One definition of done for both twins

Patterns and scale Part 05

  • Forms, lists, navigation and feedback patterns written down
  • Voice, vocabulary and message formulas
  • Ready for other languages and right-to-left
  • A plan for brands, platforms and legacy products
  • Token pipeline and lint rules automated
  • The rhythms in 27.3 in everyone's calendar

27.5Ten ways design systems fail, and the antidote

We've seen many design systems in audits. The ones that struggle almost always struggle for one of these ten reasons. None of them is about the quality of the buttons.

#How it failsThe antidoteChapter
1Built by design, ignored by engineeringGet engineering commitment before you start; staff the team with engineers02, 04
2Treated as a project, then abandonedRun it as a product, with a team that stays after launch04, 05
3Started with the fun componentsStart with an inventory and the everyday basics13
4Components before tokensTokens first, components second06
5The system team became a bottleneckContribution levels, local components and the rule of two05, 16
6Components grew forty settingsScope statements, splitting, and saying "build it locally"17, 19
7Figma and code drifted apartSame names and props; monthly twin checks; one definition of done15, 21
8Updates broke products without warningVersioning rules that include visual changes; notes; notice periods05, 22
9Nobody could find anythingA tidy library, clear names, one documentation template16
10Success measured by usage, not valueBaseline first; report time saved and change made cheap03

27.6A closing note

When we started this book, we said a design system is a shared set of decisions, reusable parts and working agreements that helps many people build one consistent product. After twenty-six chapters, we hope that sentence means a lot more than it did.

The decisions are your foundations: colours named by their job, text styles with clear roles, a spacing scale, a grid. The reusable parts are your components and patterns, designed for every state and built for everyone. And the working agreements are what keep it all alive: who owns it, how people ask for things, how changes are made safely, how you know it's working.

You don't need to do all of it at once. Pick the next stage, not the last one. Start with an audit, name your basic values, build the ten components your teams use most, and run a pilot. Then keep going, one quarter at a time, letting each step earn the next.

And whatever you build, build it so your own team can run it without outside help. That's the last of Layer One's ten rules, and the best test of whether a design system will last.

Leave the team able to run it without us.Rule #10 — Layer One

The short version

What to remember from this book

  1. A design system is an agreement, not a library: decisions, parts and the way of working together.
  2. Start small and specific: audit, tokens, the everyday components, a real pilot.
  3. Run it as a product with steady rhythms, and measure value, not just usage.
  4. Build it so your own team can run it for years.

About Layer One and the author

Layer One is a design systems studio in Bangalore, India. We set up the foundations, scale them across products and markets, and put in the governance that keeps teams using them.

Aniket Pandey

Aniket leads Layer One. His design systems work spans three very different kinds of organisation:

  • JPMorgan Chase, Senior Designer, Design Systems (2025–present): company-wide design patterns, an AI-assisted workflow for drafting them, and tooling that checks design files and code against the system, used by 500+ designers and 1,000+ engineers.
  • CARS24, Design Systems Lead (2024–25): the design system for 70+ designers and 200+ engineers, a new palette and token architecture for the rebrand, governance, and a pattern library, putting 10+ products in three countries on one token system.
  • IBM, UX Designer, design systems (2021–24): design systems for IBM clients including Cardinal Health and Riyadh Air, from foundations and tokens to governance, contribution and releases.

Source: layerone.co.in.1

The rules we work by

  1. A design system is an agreement, not a library

  2. Audit before you build

  3. Name things so people can guess them

  4. Tokens first, components second

  5. Accessible by default, not by audit

  6. Every decision comes with a reason

  7. Build where the system lives: your files, your repo

  8. Measure time saved, not usage

  9. Docs decide adoption

  10. Leave the team able to run it without us
